title: Balancing Development and Security in Global AI Governance
summary: Executive Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a core pillar of “comprehensive national power” in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), where senior officials frame the necessity of leadership in AI development as crucial for gaining an
content: Executive Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a core pillar of “comprehensive national power” in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), where senior officials frame the necessity of leadership in AI development as crucial for gaining an advantage in great power competition. Beijing is increasingly concerned about AI-related risks. Its calls for a global AI governance framework, however, are less about managing risks than about building non-Western influence in the AI domain. A recent collection of unusual People’s Daily articles on global AI governance advocate positioning the PRC as the rule-maker in the international system. None calls for cooperation with the United States, suggesting that this is not currently a priority for Beijing. Beijing is fully committed to the pursuit of supremacy in the field of artificial intelligence (AI). Officials frequently tie the technology to the country’s “comprehensive national power” (CNP; 综合国力), which Chinese leader Xi Jinping has stated must surpass that of the United States in order to achieve the Party’s primary aim of national rejuvenation ( Xinhua , September 26, 2021; China Brief , July 9). Recent articles from prominent officials and researchers have nevertheless shifted equal focus to the myriad risks associated with AI. This partly stems from very real concerns about the hard problems that rapid technological progress presents; but it is equally about the Party’s persistent preoccupation with political control and its attempts to exert more influence over the direction of international approaches to governing AI. No Slowdown in Sight A People’s Daily article from early 2025 laid out the stakes with unusual clarity. Written by an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering named Gao Wen (高 文), the article argues forcefully that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) should spare no efforts in its pursuit of AI progress.  [1] Gao describes the technology as a “core element in measuring a nation’s CNP” (衡量国家综合国力的核心要素), an “essential requirement” (必然要求) for consolidating the foundation of a strong nation, and the “strategic high ground in great power competition” (大国竞争的战略制高点). “Whoever gains the upper hand and seizes the initiative in the field of AI,” he writes, “will gain greater influence on the international stage” (谁能在人工智能领域抢占先机、赢得主动，谁就能在国际舞台上掌握更多话语权). He concludes by admonishing his readers that “opportunity knocks but once” (机不可失，时不再来), calling for “unswervingly promoting” (坚定不移地推动) the innovative development of AI ( People’s Daily , February 24, 2025). Subsequent official statements echo Gao’s analysis. A recent People’s Daily commentary, which described AI as “a strategic technology affecting a nation’s CNP” (影响国家综合国力的战略性技术), resembled quotes from politburo standing committee member Ding Xuexiang (丁薛祥) and state media describing computing power and AI talent as important manifestations of CNP (People’s Daily, May 19 , May 30 ; CCTV , June 6). Most recently, Minister for State Security Chen Yixin (陈一新), in a widely-read article for China Cyberspace Magazine , used a similar framing, saying that “whoever can seize the development opportunities of AI … will have grasped the pulse of the times” (谁能把握人工智能 …发展机遇，谁就把准了时代脉搏) ( WeChat/China Cyberspace Magazine , September 12). Theory Articles Articulate Global Governance Approach Six articles published in the People’s Daily in August underscore the extreme seriousness with which Beijing is approaching AI development and competition. What makes these articles unusual is their format. In each case, they appear in pairs, with their headlines printed vertically rather than horizontally—an editorial decision that the China Media Project has described as “a propaganda appropriation of the traditional parallel saying, or duilian (对联)” ( Substack/Lingua Sinica , August 18).  [2] These articles all focus on the global governance of AI. Each takes as its departure point a quote from Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s speech at the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference, which was held this summer in Beijing (China Brief, July 22 , August 13 ). While the first two pieces were authored by a reporter for the newspaper and appeared on the front page of the People’s Daily , the others were all commentaries published on the theory pages. The authors of these commentaries comprised the following senior personnel at important governance and research institutions: Xue Lan ( 薛澜 ): dean of the Institute for International Governance of Artificial Intelligence at Tsinghua University (co-author) Chen Ying ( 陈颖 ): special researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences Research Center for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era Wei Liang ( 魏亮 ): vice president of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) Chen Zhimin ( 陈志敏 ): researcher at the Fudan University Base of the Shanghai Research Center for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era Zhang Weiwei ( 张薇薇 ): deputy director of the Institute of World Peace and Security at the China Institute of International Studies (CIIS) The collection of theoretical commentaries trace Beijing’s global ambitions for AI governance.  [3] The first pair lays out how recent PRC actions lay the groundwork for AI to become an “international public good that benefits all of humanity” (成为造福全人类的国际公共产品), and why “Chinese wisdom” (中国智慧) offers the only viable route to international cooperation (People’s Daily, August 20, [ a ], [ b ]). The second pair, published the following week, articulates the PRC’s principles, guidance, and actions for “leading global AI governance” (引领人工智能全球治理), and frames them in relation to the country’s four global initiatives, which cover development, security, civilization, and global governance (People’s Daily, August 26, [ a ], [ b ]). Figure 1: The Theory Page of the August 20 People’s Daily The discussion of Beijing’s approach repeats many of the same points of the country’s now-familiar pitch to the world. Wei Liang provides a succinct distillation of this. He writes in his article that “China will strengthen the alignment and coordination of its AI development strategies, governance rules, and technical standards, forging a path of open consultation, multi-party participation, mutual trust, and joint governance” (中国将通过加强人工智能发展战略、治理规则、技术标准的对接协调，走出一条开放协商、多元参与的互信共治之路). Chen Zhimin then adds some specifics. He suggests that global AI governance should focus on expanding Beijing’s preferred rights—to develop, use, and benefit from AI (发展权、使用权和受益权)—and highlights several regional institutions and cooperation mechanisms to support this agenda. At the center of these is the World AI Cooperation Organization, which he says aims to “transform interim meetings and policy dialogues into regular institutional cooperation, incorporating development strategies, governance rules, technical standards, capacity building, and joint research into a relatively stable cooperation framework” (把阶段性会议和政策对话转化为常态化制度合作，把发展战略、治理规则、技术标准、能力建设和联合研究纳入相对稳定的合作框架). Setting out this ambitious agenda is ostensibly the primary purpose for these articles. At the same time, AI-related risks emerge as a dominant preoccupation of each of these expert commentators. Balancing Risks a Growing Preoccupation The Chinese government has, for nearly a decade, viewed security with the same degree of importance as development. Numerous documents published in recent years have discussed the need to balance these two sides of the governance coin (Wang, 2023).  [4] In the AI era, however, striking that balance is more challenging than ever. The government’s Artificial Intelligence Security Governance Framework 3.0 (人工智能安全治理框架3.0), released earlier this week, provides the most comprehensive list of all perceived threats AI poses ( Cyberspace Administration of China , September 14). The four theoretical commentaries, coupled with Chen Yixin’s article, all strike a concerned, if not alarmist, tone. In their article, after the introductory paragraph with its mandatory quote from Xi Jinping, Xue Lan and Chen Ying immediately turn to concerns about AI safety. They discuss the need to protect against “various endogenous and derivative risks” (各类内生和衍生风险), and to create “laws and regulations, technological supervision, risk warning, and emergency response systems, and to construct a security bottom line and prevent abuse and misuse” (法律法规、技术监测、风险预警、应急响应体系，筑牢安全底线，防范滥用恶用). Several of the authors advocate for a global governance framework precisely because of what they see as the scale of AI risks. Xue Lan and Chen Ying describe these risks as “transnational, complex, and systemic” (跨国性、复杂性和系统性), and warn that a shared vulnerability could lead to a collective failure. Wei Liang, meanwhile, writes that the danger of “risk spillover” (风险外溢) underscores the urgency of governance efforts, and he worries that AI’s increasing integration with critical infrastructure could potentially escalate into systemic risks. Zhang Weiwei similarly sees a breakthrough on governance as “urgently needed” (亟待), as the risks mean that AI governance “cannot be confined to the level of a single nation” (不能局限在单一国家层面). In a brief discussion of military applications of AI, he warns that “the relentless pursuit of asymmetric advantages through technology will exacerbate the security predicament of the international community, leading to greater insecurity and even a tragedy for all humanity” (一味追求通过技术带来不对称优势，将加重国际社会的安全困境，导致更大的不安全甚至全人类悲剧). Any workable global governance framework would need buy-in from the United States. On this point, however, the authors have little in the way of suggestions, instead choosing to recite standard critical refrains. One warns that countries that follow their own approach “harm the common interests of all countries” (损害各国共同利益). Another denounces “some countries” (个别国家) who view AI as “a tool for great power competition” (大国博弈工具), leading to “fragmentation and factionalism” (碎片化、阵营化) in global governance mechanisms. A third also implicitly criticizes the United States for attempting to “monopolize rule-making” (垄断治理规则制定权) and “increasing the difficulty of coordinating global governance” (推高全球治理的协调难度) in order to “maintain or expand [its] own advantages” (维护或扩大自身优势). This all indicates that Beijing’s bid for global AI governance is more about building power and influence outside of the West. As one scholar recently observed, the PRC seeks to build consensus among Global South countries to “unify their negotiating positions, and enhance their seats and weight in international standard setting and governance consultations” (统一谈判立场，提升其在国际标准制定与治理磋商中的席位与权重) in order to “break down technological hegemony and rule monopolies” (破除技术霸权与规则垄断) ( Wen Wei Po , July 28). Conclusion Beijing is making its pitch to lead the global governance of AI, but cooperation on AI is by no means a priority. Chen Yixin’s article shows this most clearly. Among a list of eight basic points to adhere to, international cooperation ranks last, while AI’s “strategic positioning” (战略定位) comes first; and of seven policy prescriptions he sets out, international cooperation is again bottom of the list, while pole position is given to upholding the Party’s overall leadership. This suggests that Beijing’s interpretation of AI safety differs from Western understandings in important ways. It also suggests that cooperation with Washington is not a priority that any official or Party-aligned voices are currently advocating for. Notes [1] Gao Wen is the director of Pengcheng Laboratory, which conducts AI and cyber research that could facilitate future cyberattacks or support mass surveillance, according to research by MERICS. The U.S. Commerce Department sanctioned the lab in January 2025, shortly before Gao Wen penned his commentary in the People’s Daily ( MERICS , July 3, 2025). [2] The only other instance of articles following this same format that this author has found from 2026 came on July 29, and took as their subject “new-quality productive forces” (新质生产力), Xi Jinping’s preferred formulation to describe scientific and technological advances that are intended to function as the new drivers of economic development (People’s Daily, July 29, [ a ], [ b ]). [3] David Bandurski of the China Media Project has discussed the first pair of articles, which appeared on the front page of the People’s Daily ( Substack/Lingua Sinica , August 18). Consequently, this article focuses instead on the commentaries that appeared subsequently on the newspaper’s theory pages. [4] Wang, Howard. 2023. “‘Security Is a Prerequisite for Development’: Consensus-Building toward a New Top Priority in the Chinese Communist Party.” Journal of Contemporary China 32 (142): 525–39. doi:10.1080/10670564.2022.2108681. The post Balancing Development and Security in Global AI Governance appeared first on Jamestown .

title: Costa Rica's Grynspan narrowly leads informal UN chief poll, sources say
summary: Candidate for the position of United Nations secretary-general, Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis, speaks during the "UN Town Hall: The Next Secretary-General" event at United Nations headquarters in New York City, U.S., July 23, 2026. REUTERS/Eduard
content:
Candidate for the position of United Nations secretary-general, Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis, speaks during the "UN Town Hall: The Next Secretary-General" event at United Nations headquarters in New York City, U.S., July 23, 2026. REUTERS/Eduardo Munoz [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/candidates-for-the-position-of-united-nations-secretary-general-participate-in-the-un-town-hall-the-next-secretary-general-in-new-york-city/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMlhKTUFTSUdJTQ%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

UNITED NATIONS, Sept 18 (Reuters) - An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the ​narrow frontrunner in the contest to become the 10th UN secretary-general, diplomats and other sources close ‌to the process said.

The third secret poll by the 15-member Security Council came ahead of the [annual gathering](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/why-are-world-leaders-un-next-week-and-what-will-they-talk-about-2026-09-17/) of world leaders at the United Nations in New York next week. The first poll in July showed Grynspan narrowly ahead and the second vote last month placed Guyana's UN Ambassador ​Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett in the top spot.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/misinformation-monitor/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Famericas%2Fcosta-ricas-grynspan-narrowly-leads-informal-un-chief-poll-sources-say-2026-09-18%2F)

Eight [candidates](https://www.reuters.com/world/who-are-candidates-running-un-secretary-general-2026-08-21/)are vying to succeed Antonio Guterres, who steps down at the end of ​this year after two five-year terms. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the ⁠race.

Richard Gowan, director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, said neither Grynspan nor Rodrigues Birkett seem ​to be able to make a decisive breakthrough and "it is time for some the weaker candidates to bow out of ​the race."

"I think these figures may encourage any additional candidates who are waiting in the wings to jump into the race quite soon," said Gowan.

Ultimately the five Security Council veto powers - the United States, China, Russia, France and Britain - need to agree on a candidate. When Guterres ​was chosen in 2016, it took six straw polls for the Security Council to reach agreement.

The UN Security Council will eventually formally ​recommend a candidate to the 193-member General Assembly for election. The approval by the assembly has long been seen as a rubber stamp.

## FRIDAY'S NUMBERS

In the ‌Security ⁠Council straw polls, which are expected to continue for several more rounds, Security Council members are asked on secret ballots if they "encourage," "discourage" or have "no opinion" on candidates.

Grynspan received nine encourage, five discourage and one no opinion and Rodrigues Birkett received eight encourage, six discourage and one no opinion, diplomats and sources close to the process said.

In the more than 80-year history of ​the United Nations there has never ​been a female secretary-general.

Uganda's ⁠Olara Otunnu, a diplomat and former U.N. under-secretary-general, received five encourage, seven discourage and three no opinion; Argentina's Rafael Grossi, the high-profile director general of the U.N. nuclear watchdog, received ​five encourage, eight discourage and two no opinion; while Senegal's former president Macky Sall received ​five encourage, nine ⁠discourage and one no opinion.

Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a former Ecuadorean foreign and defence minister and former president of the UN General Assembly, received three encourage, six discourage and six no opinion; Michelle Bachelet, a two-time president of Chile and a former UN ⁠High Commissioner ​for Human Rights, received one encourage, 11 discourage and three no opinion; ​while Ivonne Baki, an Ecuadorean diplomat, received zero encourage, 10 discourage and five no opinion.

Reporting by David Brunnstrom in Washington, Olivia Le Poidevin and Emma ​Farge in Geneva, Francois Murphy in Vienna and Michelle Nichols at the United Nations; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Chizu Nomiyama

title: 所有人担心AI失控，特朗普和习近平能就必要护栏达成协议吗？
summary: 华盛顿 — 人工智能(AI)正日益成为华盛顿与北京战略与经济竞争的焦点。如何管控AI风险，不仅将是美国财政部长斯科特·贝森特(Scott Bessent)本周末与中国国务院副总理何立峰会晤时讨论的议题之一，预计也将成为唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)总统下星期在华盛顿与中国国家主席习近平举行峰会时的重点议题之一。在AI领域日益激烈的竞争美中两国，能否在降低这项技术潜在风险方面达成协议，防范风险？ **为什么重要？**前沿AI模型正以令人警惕的速度取得进展，其中包括前
content:
华盛顿 —

人工智能(AI)正日益成为华盛顿与北京战略与经济竞争的焦点。如何管控AI风险，不仅将是美国财政部长斯科特·贝森特(Scott Bessent)本周末与中国国务院副总理何立峰会晤时讨论的议题之一，预计也将成为唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)总统下星期在华盛顿与中国国家主席习近平举行峰会时的重点议题之一。在AI领域日益激烈的竞争美中两国，能否在降低这项技术潜在风险方面达成协议，防范风险？

**为什么重要？**前沿AI模型正以令人警惕的速度取得进展，其中包括前所未有的进攻性网络能力。近期美国AI公司OpenAI 和Anthropic先后出现的内部AI模型突破隔离措施，入侵第三方系统的事件，更加剧了必须管控AI风险的紧迫感。美中两个AI大国还未就这一影响深远的技术举行真正意义上的对话。

美国信息技术和创新基金会(ITIF)创办人和前总裁罗伯特·阿特金森(Robert Atkinson)近日在接受美国之音采访时说，美中需要在这方面携手合作，虽然阿特金森认为美中正陷入技术、科技和贸易战中。

“这是我们两国可以合作的领域，因为目前还没有其他国家像美国和中国那样在人工智能领域投入如此多的资源。我们是领导者。所以我们需要在这方面携手合作。”他说。

今年5月，特朗普总统访问北京期间，与中国国家主席习近平就启动两国人工智能政府间对话达成一致意见。但在习近平下个星期访问美国前，双方还没有公开确认已经举行过此类会谈。

**最新进展**

*   财政部长贝森特星期三表示，他周末在纽约与中国国务院副总理何立峰会晤时，美国愿意就避免AI的“共同风险”进行讨论。

“美国仍然是人工智能领域的领导者，我们愿意就如何避免共同风险和避免两国系统分裂进行讨论。我们希望讨论能够涵盖开放式和封闭式权重模型。”贝森特星期三在给美国媒体Axios的一份声明中表示。

*   众议院中共问题特设委员会首席民主党成员，来自加利福尼亚州的民主党籍众议员罗·卡纳(Ro Khanna)同一天致函中国阿里巴巴集团首席执行官及董事吴泳铭和阿里巴巴集团董事局主席蔡崇信敦促他们与美国领先的AI实验室达成“一项具有约束力、可执行且可验证的协议，以引领人工智能前沿发展”。

他在信中写道：“Anthropologie、OpenAI和xAI的首席执行官们在很多问题上存在分歧，但本月初，他们齐聚一堂，一致认为我们应该放慢人工智能的发展速度，直到社会能够建立必要的安全保障措施。现在，月之暗面(Moonshot)、阿里巴巴和深度求索(DeepSeek)也应该这样做。”

**美中都担忧AI失控**

美中两国近期都对日益强大的AI可能带来的重大风险表达了担忧，虽然关注重点有所不同。美国更强调AI对人类安全可能造成的风险，包括技术失控及其潜在安全影响；中国则更关注AI可能带来的政治安全和社会稳定风险。

9月12日，美国人工智能公司Anthropic联合创始人达里奥·阿莫迪(Dario Amodei)发文呼吁放慢前沿AI模型能力的提升速度以预留安全研究时间。

这项名为“控制AI发展节奏”(Pace The Frontier)的运动得到获得了OpenAI首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼(Sam Altman)、 xAI的埃隆·马斯克(Elon Musk)和谷歌DeepMind的德米斯·哈萨比斯(Demis Hassabis)等其他AI公司高管的支持。

9月13日，中国国家安全部长陈一新发表文章称人工智能正以前所未有的速度、广度和深度渗透人类社会。他在文章中提到了AI可能带来的六大风险，其中最主要的风险是对中国共产党的潜在威胁。共产党担心这项技术可能被用于攻击自身，并已实施意识形态控制，以确保产品符合社会主义价值观。

9月17日，中国国安部发布视频揭示今年5月至6月，OpenAI公司相关的AI智能体在执行测试任务期间，“劫持”了德国程序员维基网站，建立“地下论坛”的事情。视频指出：“当AI智能体被赋予越来越多的现实行动能力，技术迭代与安全围栏之间的缝隙，正在悄然扩大”。

在同一天闭幕的北京香山论坛上，与会的多国代表也对AI不受控制的发展和美中在此领域的竞争表达担忧。

**特朗普总统怎么说？**

特朗普总统拒绝美国科技界要求放缓人工智能发展的呼声。9月13日，特朗普在被问及人工智能行业是否应该放缓发展速度或面临更严格的监管时表示，“谁赢了人工智能，谁就赢了。”不过，他赞同阿莫迪等高管的观点，即美国必须通过出口管制和其他措施来维持其在人工智能领域对中国的领先地位。

9月14日，他在真相社交上发帖称，“针对人工智能和数据中心有一个病态的阴谋(sick conspiracy)，而唯一会对此感到高兴的是中国。” 他还再次强调，“谁掌握人工智能，谁就赢了！” 他还表示，美国政府已经对AI公司拥有巨大的刑事和监管权。

7月23日，特朗普公布了一项人工智能行动计划。该计划旨在推动美国人工智能产业发展，并在全球人工智能技术领域赢得领先地位，超越美国的对手中国。

特朗普还表示，他的政府希望将美国打造成为“人工智能出口强国”，包括扩大美国芯片、软件和数据存储技术的出口。

**美国国会看法**

值得指出的是，对AI发展该放慢脚步或大步前行，美国会两党议员分歧明显。反对者的一个担忧就是，美国不能将AI的未来拱手让给中国。美国需要采取措施应对潜在风险，但需要在人工智能领域保持领先。

众议院美国与中国共产党战略竞争特设委员会主席约翰·穆勒纳尔(John Moolenaar)星期五(9月18日)致函特朗普总统，敦促他加倍采取措施，阻止中国获取美国人工智能技术的核心。他警告说，中国决心与美国的人工智能体系脱钩。

“中国政府一方面拒绝允许中国的人工智能实验室合法购买他们急需的美国技术，另一方面却允许他们非法获取这些资源。这传递出的信息很明确：中国决心与美国的人工智能体系脱钩。”他在信中写道。

他说，这显示中国并非是一个长期的市场。他建议加强对人工智能的管控，堵住漏洞，尽可能减缓中国人工智能的发展速度。

关于美中竞争，尤其是在人工智能方面的竞争，美国国会下属的美中经济与安全审查委员会(USCC)民主党委员克里斯·斯莱文(Chris Slevin)这样告诉美国之音(VOA)：

“我认为我们看到这种竞争更多地体现在供应链和技术领域，尤其是在人工智能方面。正如之前提到的，我们非常重视前沿人工智能。那么，如何在竞争中脱颖而出？竞争究竟是什么样的？我们现在发现，这并非一场线性竞争或竞赛，而是强调开源、人工智能和部署，以及真正地收集数据来推动创新。我认为这与美国过去几年在类似模型以及芯片、硬件和能源方面的侧重点有所不同。多年来，美国一直关注着类似的模型以及相关的芯片、硬件和能源。这是我们委员会一直关注的领域。

他7月份曾经随着USCC的一个代表团访问了北京。他说，就技术而言，我们在访问期间听到的是，中国对自身在人工智能前沿领域的进展及其部署战略充满信心。而且，听起来中国有兴趣与美国探讨某种双边人工智能对话。

**习近平的看法**

9月12日至13日，在印度举行的金砖国家领导人峰会上， 习近平希望“金砖国家要牢牢把握主动权，加强人工智能合作”。 另外，中国还将开源人工智能模型视为外交工具，并一直将其推广为一项全球“公共产品”，在金砖峰会上，习近平向金砖国家11个成员国表示，愿意帮助它们发展开源人工智能，并敦促它们加入中国的全球人工智能治理倡议。

早在2018年，习近平就强调，人工智能是引领这一轮科技革命和产业变革的战略性技术，具有溢出带动性很强的“头雁”效应。后来，他又多次表示，中国要占领先机、赢得优势。

习近平也对人工智能的安全性表达过担忧。7月，在中国上海举行的世界人工智能大会上，习近平在主旨讲话中强调，对人工智能的发展要“强化风险意识，确保安全可控”。 他指出，人工智能应该成为“人类的可信工具”。

中国的“十五五”规划(2026—2030年)表示将全面实施“人工智能+”行动，把人工智能定位为引领新一轮科技革命和产业变革的核心引擎。

**近期交锋**

美中近期在人工智能领域的直接交锋也越来越激烈。

9月8日，美国三家政府机构指控六家中国公司利用“蒸馏”技术恶意抄袭美国AI产品，执法官员在一份声明中指出，这些中国公司此举“很可能是在中国政府知情的情况下进行的”。

此前，美国官员和美国AI公司也曾指责中国 人工智能公司非法蒸馏美国公司的模型。

当时，美国财政部长贝森特提出，如果发现中国人工智能企业通过“蒸馏”等方式窃取美国企业技术成果，美国政府不排除对其实施制裁 。而中国商务部则批评相关主张体现了双重标准和人工智能霸权主义。

7月28日，美国联邦通信委员会(FCC)正式将先进机器人和联网型电力逆变器列入“受管制清单”，禁止其获得进入美国市场所需的设备认证。

在此之前，中国工业和信息化部网络安全威胁和漏洞信息共享平台(NVDB)称Anthropic公司的Claude模型存在安全后门隐患，阿里巴巴宣布禁止在内部使用该模型。

**关注重点：**鉴于两国之间缺乏互信以及激烈的竞争，作为全球人工智能领域最具影响力的两个国家，美中能否和应当如何应对人类可能失去对最先进前沿AI模型控制的风险？

华盛顿智库战略与国际研究中心高级顾问甘思德(Scott Kennedy)告诉美国之音，本次峰会中，两国能否在AI会谈上取得进展，是他关注的重点之一。“会不会事先讨论人工智能，并在峰会上把双方较低层级已经谈过的内容提出来，为后续如何处理人工智能设定议程。”他说。

**最有可能的结果，美国专家意见：**

*   美国智库卡内基国际和平研究院技术与国际事务项目研究员、中国AI倡议共同主任斯科特·辛格(Scott Singer)9月15日在一个有关全球智能体人工智能防护措施的研讨会上说，美中是两个利益诉求截然不同、对这些技术所带来的风险也有着不同认知的国家，对他们来说，要达成任何形式的协议，特别是建立真正能够执行这一协议的技术基础设施，都需要时间，但，两国应该还是可以取得进展的。

辛格说：“你通常不会看到一个一蹴而就的重大协议。它需要时间，随着信任的建立和技术的发展而逐步实现。对于人工智能这样发展如此迅速的技术来说，我认为现在就让我们陷入一个可能在六个月后就不再合理的协议是不负责任的。因此，我们这次会议真正能做的，也是我们应该期盼的，是建立一个专门用于管理人工智能风险的永久渠道，并与一线技术专家建立清晰的联系，以便进行具体、真实的对话，理想情况下，还要使之与美中关系的起伏波动脱钩。” 他说。他补充说，要达到这一点，需要双方都展现出高超的外交技巧。

*   华盛顿智库战略与国际研究中心AI中心主任亚洛克·梅塔(Aalok Mehta)9月17日在该中心有关特习会的研讨会上说，最有可能的进展方式是就一些具体问题进行讨论。

“首先是明确人工智能安全开发的定义，以及一些基本的安全措施。其次，建立一条沟通热线，以便美中两国就新兴或正在发展的人工智能问题进行沟通。第三，更具体地讨论网络安全事件。我认为这很可能是峰会能取得的最切实成果。例如，美国政府同意加强对美国公司造成的网络安全事件的监控，中国政府同意加强对中国公司造成的网络安全事件的监控，然后建立某种信息共享机制，双方政府在对敏感信息进行编辑后，再将信息发送给对方。”

*   华盛顿智库保卫民主基金会(FDD)高级研究员格雷格·辛格尔顿(Craig Singleton)认为目前关于人工智能的对话被过度炒作了。他说，北京确实意识到人工智能对中共政权构成的潜在风险，但这并不意味着中国希望与美国在人工智能领域建立类似核武器的军控机制。考虑到，中国也在努力加快其人工智能模型的推广，构建全球开源生态系统，并扩大中国人工智能在海外的应用，中国不可能希望达成一项限制能力增长或减缓技术扩散的协议。

“或许在滥用和网络安全、生物安全或自主系统等领域存在一些非常狭窄的重叠，但我几乎看不到任何证据表明北京希望达成一项限制能力增长或减缓技术扩散的协议。这些恰恰是中国认为具有战略机遇的领域。”

*   曾经共同主导首轮美中人工智能对话的前国务院特使塞斯·森特(Seth Center)在9月17日在《纽约时报》撰文认为，会谈不太可能有效，因为“中国不在乎人工智能的安全，它只想赢”。

他在文章中写道，“我担心即将举行的会谈无法拯救我们。如果历史可以作为参考，那么除了获取竞争优势，中国对其他任何事情都不会太感兴趣。”

他解释说，2024年5月那次会议的议程对双方而言都极为明确，因为两国元首已对此达成一致：重点关注高级人工智能系统的风险及安全合作的潜力。然而，在长达数小时的时间里，中方官员一直回避人工智能系统的潜在风险问题。他们甚至不愿解释其国内的人工智能法规，尽管现场就有监管官员。相反，中国将美国的安全策略描绘成阻碍释放技术机遇的屏障，以及阻止较贫穷国家获取人工智能工具的手段。

title: Why Eurasia, Not the Indo-Pacific, Matters Most in Next Phase of Taiwan Deterrence
summary: Why Eurasia, Not the Indo-Pacific, Matters Most in Next Phase of Taiwan Deterrence bbert@hudson.org Fri, 09/18/2026 - 09:56 SVG Commentary Sep 18, 2026 War on the Rocks Why Eurasia, Not the Indo-Pacific, Matters Most in Next Phase of Taiwan
content: Why Eurasia, Not the Indo-Pacific, Matters Most in Next Phase of Taiwan Deterrence bbert@hudson.org Fri, 09/18/2026 - 09:56 SVG Commentary Sep 18, 2026 War on the Rocks Why Eurasia, Not the Indo-Pacific, Matters Most in Next Phase of Taiwan Deterrence Ken Moriyasu Senior Fellow William Pazos Ken Moriyasu & William Pazos Commentary Caption Chinese President Xi Jinping walks past Kyrgyz honour guards during a welcoming ceremony prior to talks with his Kyrgyzstan's counterpart in Bishkek on August 31, 2026. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print Washington is preparing for the right war, but in the wrong theater. For years, U.S. strategic thinking has centered on the Indo‑Pacific : the militarized atolls of the South China Sea, China’s churning naval shipyards , and the tense waters of the Taiwan Strait. Yet the next phase of competition will likely play out on the Eurasian landmass, contested through pipelines, swing states, and shifting alignments along routes that overlap with the ancient Silk Road. This is where China is building alternative trade and energy corridors beyond the immediate reach of U.S. military power. Chinese strategists have long worried that, in a conflict over Taiwan, the United States could exploit China’s dependence on seaborne energy and trade by closing the Strait of Malacca — the narrow waterway between Malaysia and Indonesia, through which roughly 75 to 80 percent of China’s seaborne oil imports pass. Beijing has sought to overcome this vulnerability by building a multi-dimensional transportation network across land and sea . Recent disruptions in and around the Strait of Hormuz have underscored the urgency of this effort. The objective is not to replace maritime trade with overland trade. Rather, greater confidence in China’s ability to withstand maritime disruption could embolden Beijing to take greater risks over Taiwan. Without adjusting to this reality, the United States and its allies risk concentrating too narrowly on the maritime contest. To shape the trajectory of U.S.-Chinese competition, Washington ought to understand both China’s maritime and continental strategies. Escaping Chokepoints As early as 2005, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences scholar Zhang Jie explicitly connected China’s vulnerability at the Strait of Malacca to its freedom of action over Taiwan. U.S. efforts to control the strait, she argued, not only posed a potential threat to China’s energy security but also constrained Beijing’s “ability to act on the Taiwan issue and in neighboring affairs.” Her proposed solution was to bypass Southeast Asia and to open new petroleum transportation routes through Central Asia and Russia. Zhang, now director of the Asia-Pacific security and diplomacy division at the Academy, noted in The Malacca Factor in China’s Energy Security that Beijing’s early attempts to bypass the Strait of Malacca — such as constructing a canal across Thailand’s Kra Isthmus or building oil and gas pipelines through Myanmar — were insufficient to resolve the “Malacca Dilemma.” While such projects would allow ships to avoid the strait itself, Zhang argued that none “can genuinely eliminate the possibility of intervention by major powers.” Malacca was but a microcosm of China’s maritime oil transportation predicament. Instead, she called for strengthening energy cooperation with Central Asia and Russia. Zhang acknowledged that the then-planned China-Kazakhstan oil pipeline and the prospective oil and gas routes from Russia could not replace the Middle East’s role in China’s energy supplies for a considerable period. But she argued that the overland routes would possess “greater strategic significance under non-peacetime conditions.” She continued: “They would therefore possess a relatively high degree of security and would be less susceptible to influence by Western countries.” Two decades later, much of the infrastructure Zhang envisioned exists. China has also built the Central Asia-China gas pipeline from Turkmenistan, whose three existing lines have a capacity of 55 billion cubic meters per year. A planned fourth line would increase that capacity to 85 billion cubic meters. If Beijing were also to agree to Russia’s proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline , with another 50 billion cubic meters of annual capacity, China would gain the ability to substitute overland gas for a substantial share of the liquefied natural gas it currently imports by sea. Rather than eliminating its dependence on seaborne energy, China seems to be building enough resilience — through overland pipelines, storage, and demand flexibility — to withstand a serious disruption at sea. Renmin University Professor Cui Shoujun describes the pipelines as a solid “energy security barrier,” China’s shift to renewable energy as establishing a strategic “moat,” and technologies that convert coal into oil and methanol as an additional “safety net” against fuel and petrochemical feedstock shortages in extreme circumstances. How resilient has China become? Some say that China’s sharp reduction of seaborne crude oil imports during this Iran crisis may have amounted to a “ dry run ” for a Malacca blockade. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, China imported just 8.1 million barrels per day of crude oil in the second quarter of 2026, 32 percent less than in the previous quarter. Yet China did not make up the difference simply by emptying its strategic reserves. The Energy Information Administration estimates that China’s strategic inventories declined by just 49 million barrels during the quarter, from 1.54 billion to 1.49 billion barrels. Beijing absorbed much of the shock by reducing the amount of oil its refineries processed rather than replacing every lost imported barrel from storage. This does not mean China could withstand a wartime blockade indefinitely. If China tried to replace a 3.9 million barrel-per-day import shortfall entirely from a 1.49 billion barrel stockpile, those stocks would last roughly a year. But the Hormuz episode shows why such arithmetic can exaggerate China’s vulnerability. Beijing can respond to a supply shock by rationing petroleum use as well as drawing down reserves. In wartime, it could ration more aggressively, preserving fuel for the military while forcing deeper cuts elsewhere in the economy. Beijing is signaling that it wants further resilience. In August, China’s National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration released their new five-year plan for oil and natural gas development , calling explicitly for China to “consolidate and expand strategic overland import corridors” and pursue a diversified import strategy. There has been ample debate over whether the United States could actually blockade China’s maritime trade. In a 2008 Naval War College Review paper , Gabriel Collins and William Murray identified several critical challenges: where to marshal seized vessels, how to handle multinational crews, how to determine which tankers were carrying oil for China, and how to prevent tankers from simply taking alternative routes such as through the Lombok and Sunda straits. Sean Mirski, meanwhile, argued in 2013 that a U.S. naval blockade could impose ruinous costs on China in a prolonged conflict, especially if it was accompanied by a coalition including Russia, India, and Japan to prevent Beijing from circumventing the blockade through alternative maritime and overland routes. Russia’s alignment with China makes one of Mirski’s key conditions harder to achieve and elevates the importance of the remaining states along China’s continental periphery. But regardless of the blockade debate in the West, Chinese strategists will assume the worst and prepare accordingly. Rethinking the Indian Ocean In 2010, Robert Kaplan predicted that the Indian Ocean would become the central arena of global competition, driven partly by China’s dependence on energy crossing Hormuz and Malacca and growing Sino-Indian rivalry. Sixteen years later, that prediction looks less certain. The U.S. Indo-Pacific Command has reverted to Pacific Command — a change that Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s policy chief, has described as underscoring the focus on the Pacific element of the First Island Chain. The Quad — the United States, Japan, India, and Australia, often treated as the premier gathering of Indo-Pacific leaders — has not held a leaders’ summit in nearly two years. While India is a massive player on the world stage, its ability to shape China’s continental strategy is limited by geography. Over a century ago, British geographer Halford Mackinder observed that China proper and India are separated by “the most massive uplands on the Globe,” the Himalaya Range and the Tibetan Plateau, which is “as large as France, Germany, and Austria-Hungary put together.” The geography has not changed. With no realistic plans for pipelines or railroads across that terrain, Chinese strategists have looked instead to Central Asia, where geography is far more conducive to overland connectivity. Xi’s Continental Turn In September 2013, China’s top leader Xi Jinping launched his signature infrastructure project , the Belt and Road Initiative , in Astana, Kazakhstan. He declared that relations with Central Asia would become a priority of Chinese foreign policy. A month later, Xi convened a foreign policy work conference specifically on the theme of China’s “periphery diplomacy,” the first such themed forum since the establishment of the People’s Republic of China in 1949. “We need to help neighbors in times of crisis, treat them as equals, visit them frequently, and take actions that will win us support and friendship,” Xi said . A dozen years later, in April 2025, Xi convened the Central Conference on Work Related to Neighboring Countries, once again doubling down on neighborhood diplomacy as a guiding principle of foreign policy. The timing was symbolic, coming just days after U.S. President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs on his “Liberation Day.” At the end of the road lies Xi’s ambition: the Chinese Dream of the “ great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation .” It pledges that by 2049 China will be prosperous, strong , and globally leading — with “ socialism with Chinese characteristics ” vindicated as history’s winner. As U.K.-based China specialists Steve Tsang and Olivia Cheung argue, the crowning achievement of this rejuvenation would be the subjugation of Taiwan, a spectacular move meant to expose American strategic inability. It would be the end of Pax Americana and the beginning of a Sino-centric order, a Pax Sinica . Malacca on Land If we are right, the key to deterrence may be to complicate Beijing’s assumptions about the security and reliability of the continental corridors on which its long‑term strategy depends. Washington should deepen diplomatic engagement with the Eurasian countries that sit astride the energy and trade corridors Beijing is trying to establish across the continent. Three are particularly important to China’s overland connectivity. Kazakhstan, with its long, flat terrain and extensive rail network, offers China a stable overland route to the Caspian region. Uzbekistan, true to its Silk Road heritage, is set to become a key transit hub when the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway comes online. Once in Uzbekistan, the Chinese-built rail link will connect onward to Turkmenistan and Iran. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, controls one of Eurasia’s most important trade choke points, known as the Ganja Gap . The Hudson Institute’s Luke Coffey notes that overland trade between Asia and Europe seeking to avoid Russia and Iran must pass through the narrow corridor connecting Azerbaijan with Georgia. Only about 60 kilometers wide at its narrowest point, the Ganja Gap carries an extraordinary concentration of strategic infrastructure. Oil and gas pipelines, the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway, and other critical infrastructure all pass through the corridor. Its importance extends far beyond Azerbaijan. To the west, the corridor opens through Georgia and Turkey toward the Black Sea, the Mediterranean, and Europe. To the east, it reaches across the Caspian toward Kazakhstan and the rest of Central Asia — and ultimately China. The Ganja Gap is the narrow hinge connecting the trans-Caspian Middle Corridor on either side of the Caucasus. It is, in effect, Malacca on land. These corridor states are not Chinese satellites. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Azerbaijan are quintessential “swing states,” cultivating relations with competing powers rather than committing themselves exclusively to either side. Their willingness to work with both Washington and Beijing was apparent when their leaders attended China’s military parade in Beijing last September and the U.S.-led Board of Peace launch ceremony in Davos in January. They are part of a broader belt of Eurasian swing states whose decisions on infrastructure, energy and diplomatic alignment will help determine whether China’s continental strategy unfolds in a permissive or contested environment. Countering Belt and Road In addition to diplomatic outreach, Washington must offer credible economic alternatives to Chinese financing. Previous efforts to compete with the Belt and Road Initiative — such as the Blue Dot Network — struggled to gain traction, mostly because the money involved paled beside China’s program. An alternative may already be on the table. What if the investment commitments Trump secured in trade deals with the European Union , Japan , and South Korea to reduce tariffs — worth $600 billion, $550 billion, and $350 billion, respectively — could be mobilized? Those commitments are currently intended for investment in the United States. But the Trump administration should consider renegotiating the agreements to allow a portion of the commitments to finance strategic projects in third countries. Japan, whose $550 billion commitment is proving particularly difficult to deploy, offers the clearest test case. If successful, the model could eventually be extended to other trade-deal commitments. The U.S.-Japanese arrangement emerged from an unusually informal and intensely personal negotiation between Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Japanese trade envoy Ryosei Akazawa. Akazawa repeatedly flew to Washington — at times without a meeting firmly scheduled — and waited for opportunities to negotiate with Lutnick, later describing the talks as a fight to protect Japanese interests. The resulting framework was repeatedly adjusted as the two sides worked out its terms. It was a product of bargaining rather than an immutable legal architecture, and there is no reason why the bargaining could not continue. For Japan, such a change could be a blessing in disguise. Under the current arrangement , Japan provides the financing, while project cash flows are divided equally between Japan and the United States until Tokyo recovers its allocation. That structure dramatically lengthens the time required for Japan to recoup its money. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis calculates that, under a simplified scenario in which a project yields 10 percent annually, Japan would require 20 years to recover its initial investment. Without the 50-50 split, the same investment would take 10 years. Unsurprisingly, projects that can plausibly remain profitable over 20 years are limited. Energy infrastructure has therefore figured prominently among the six projects, worth $109 billion, announced so far. But announcements have stalled, leaving Japan struggling to identify enough viable projects to fulfill its $550 billion commitment by the end of Trump’s term. Washington, meanwhile, wants the full $550 billion deployed. The two governments could establish a limited third-country window for projects they jointly designate as advancing American and Japanese economic security. Japanese capital could finance critical mineral, energy, and transportation infrastructure in Central Asia and the Caucasus, where commercially viable projects could simultaneously reduce Chinese and Russian leverage. Denying China the Interior If Beijing becomes less confident about its continental periphery, it may become less willing to take military risks elsewhere. The point is not to turn Central Asia or the Caucasus into formal allies. It is to deny China confidence that the interior of Eurasia will function as a sanctuary. This does not mean integrating Kazakhstan into NATO or rapidly expanding arms sales across the heart of Asia. It means making Beijing think twice. Injecting complicated, multi‑vector choices into Chinese decision‑making can help prevent the fait accompli seizure of Taiwan that American planners worry about — and do so far more cost‑effectively than pressuring allies to double and triple defense budgets . China needs confidence that its continental trade and energy routes would remain reliable in a crisis. But Kazakhstan’s response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 should give Beijing pause. Only a month earlier, Russian-led forces from the Collective Security Treaty Organization had deployed at President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s request during the worst domestic unrest since Kazakhstan’s independence. Yet this extraordinary security assistance from Russia did not translate into obedience once Russia went to war. Tokayev refused to recognize the Russian-backed entities in Donetsk and Luhansk and publicly pledged that Kazakhstan would not violate Western sanctions. Kazakhstan did not sever its relationship with Russia. Instead, Tokayev sought to preserve the country’s multi-vector foreign policy and avoid excessive dependence on Moscow. Washington should not expect Kazakhstan or other Central Asian states to cut trade or energy ties with China over Taiwan. Yet Kazakhstan’s response to Russia demonstrates that dependence on a powerful neighbor does not necessarily mean acquiescence. The more alternatives these states have, the greater their ability to resist pressure from Beijing when their interests diverge. Furthermore, recent U.S. diplomatic initiatives in Central Asia — new corridors , new formats , and new partnerships — have begun to insert American influence into the very interior on which China relies. Central Asian embassies are actively discussing with the administration an invitation for Trump to visit the region next year. He would be the first sitting American president to visit Central Asia. A photo of Trump standing in Registan Square in Samarkand alongside Central Asian leaders would send an unmistakable message to Beijing: The United States is on the Silk Road too. If the Indo‑Pacific is where a Taiwan war would be fought, Eurasia is where Beijing is shaping the conditions under which it would choose to fight. Washington should adjust its strategy accordingly. summary: U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression kfisher Fri, 09/18/2026 - 17:26 On Releases & Statements U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression Washington, DC – The U.S. Commission on Interna
content: U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression kfisher Fri, 09/18/2026 - 17:26 On Releases & Statements     U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression  Washington, DC – The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom ( USCIRF ) has reported for years that China’s violations of freedom of religion or belief (FoRB) have been too numerous to count and too heinous to ignore. USCIRF asks President Donald J. Trump to directly raise with President Xi Jinping China’s systematic, ongoing, and egregious violations of FoRB during the U.S.-China summit in Washington, D.C. on September 24, 2026.  “ The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), under the leadership of President Xi, has undertaken a genocidal campaign against Uyghurs and other Turkic minorities. It has attempted to eliminate or take complete control of Tibetan Buddhism, and it threatens the free succession of the Dalai Lama ,” said Commissioner  David A. Anderson . “ It has arrested independent Protestant church leaders and breached China’s protocols with the Catholic Church. It has attempted to separate ethnic Mongolians from their religious and cultural traditions. It has harassed and imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners, Church of Almighty God members, and followers of other religious and belief communities. And it has carried out a campaign of transnational repression far beyond its borders, including within the United States of America .”  In July, a wide-ranging Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, which represents the forced imposition of CCP ideology and ethnonationalist supremacy over all of China’s diverse ethnic and religious groups, took effect across China. It codifies into Chinese law an even more comprehensive and totalitarian system of repression of religious freedom while declaring that the CCP has the authority to pursue organizations and individuals outside of China for undermining the new law.   “ The Ethnic Unity and Progress Law has raised alarms across the international community, requests for clarification from UN special rapporteurs, and concerns from U.S. lawmakers ,” said Commissioner  Gene Mills . “ USCIRF asks President Trump to use this crucial opportunity of direct talks with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi, to bolster U.S. interests and priorities by advancing religious freedom for all of China’s people .”  USCIRF recommended in its  2026 Annual Report  that the U.S. Department of State keep China on the Country of Particular Concern (CPC) list for engaging in systematic, ongoing, and egregious violations of religious freedom. USCIRF raised China’s abysmal religious freedom conditions during its “FoRB Violations Against Christians Abroad” hearing in January and in its “China’s Codification and Escalation of the ‘Sinicization of Religion’”  publication  in May. ###  The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) is an independent, bipartisan legislative branch agency established by the U.S. Congress to monitor, analyze, and report on religious freedom abroad. USCIRF makes foreign policy recommendations to the President, the Secretary of State, and Congress, intended to deter religious persecution and promote freedom of religion and belief. To interview a commissioner, please contact USCIRF at  media@uscirf.gov .   Fri, 09/18/2026 - 17:26 News Press Releases & Statements Related Country China

title: US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
summary: The U.S. government has long warned, in sweeping terms, that the Chinese tech giant Huawei is effectively an arm of the Chinese state that acts with impunity on the global stage, including allegedly violating U.S. sanctions. Over the last t
content: The U.S. government has long warned, in sweeping terms, that the Chinese tech giant Huawei is effectively an arm of the Chinese state that acts with impunity on the global stage, including allegedly violating U.S. sanctions. Over the last two weeks, U.S. prosecutors have begun to make that case, labeling Huawei a “criminal enterprise,” in what could be a lengthy trial in a New York federal court. Huawei enacted “a far-reaching criminal scheme extending over twenty years,” according to Department of Justice prosecutor Taylor Stout. “Crime was an important business strategy.” Nearly eight years after the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed its indictment against Huawei, the company is facing 12 felony charges, including that it conspired to steal technologies from U.S. competitors and business partners. The federal government also alleges that Huawei lied to its Western banking partners about doing business in Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions. No individuals have been charged. Huawei’s lawyers rejected the government’s characterization, with Brian Heberlig, one of at least a dozen attorneys working for the defense, arguing that the charges concerned “disconnected incidents.” “It’s about competition, not conspiracy,” Heberlig said. In December 2018, Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Vancouver at the request of U.S. officials and charged with fraud. After a lengthy period of house arrest, Meng reached a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. authorities in 2021 in which she admitted to lying to HSBC and other banks about a Huawei subsidiary’s business in Iran. That admission will likely be introduced during the trial. As reported in China Capital , ICIJ’s recent investigation into Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Huawei had leaned on its close relations with the state-owned bank to insulate itself from the fallout of Meng’s arrest. After the Justice Department unveiled its indictment, the company’s bankers at ICBC’s London branch facilitated a transfer of $1.3 billion in “emergency cash” from London to a branch in China without informing compliance staff. https://www.icij.org/investigations/china-capital/china-banking-icbc-oligarchs-sanctions-london/ OVERVIEW Chinese banking giant serves firms linked to oligarchs and autocrats to push Beijing’s agenda Sep 14, 2026 https://www.icij.org/investigations/china-capital/huawei-icbc-banking-us-court-beijing-london/ HUAWEI Chinese bank helped Huawei spirit $1B out of London days after US indictment of the tech giant Sep 14, 2026 https://www.icij.org/investigations/china-capital/about-china-capital-investigation-icbc/ Asia-Pacific About the China Capital investigation Sep 14, 2026 Recommended reading OVERVIEW Chinese banking giant serves firms linked to oligarchs and autocrats to push Beijing’s agenda Sep 14, 2026 HUAWEI Chinese bank helped Huawei spirit $1B out of London days after US indictment of the tech giant Sep 14, 2026 Asia-Pacific About the China Capital investigation Sep 14, 2026

content: 美国官员表示，情报官员在内部报告中就中国可能针对向沙特阿拉伯出售数十架先进F-35战斗机一事进行间谍活动表达了担忧。这笔 待完成的军售 价值240亿美元。 这些美国官员说，情报分析人士指出，中国可能通过在沙特阿拉伯的间谍活动，或通过其与沙特的军事和安全伙伴关系获取F-35战机技术。 一名官员说，五角大楼国防情报局数月前发布了一份详细报告，讨论了中国军方进入沙特基地以及沙特在电信基础设施中使用中国技术的问题。这名官员说，报告还质疑美沙两国能否维持F-35技术所在设施的安全。 这份报告以及来自其他情报机构的评估已在几个政府机构和国会办公室之间传阅。2025年秋，在政府讨论这笔军售可能性时，国防情报局曾就类似风险发布过一份更笼统的报告，《纽约时报》当时对此进行了 报道 。 随后，特朗普总统在于11月在白宫接待沙特王储穆罕默德·本·萨勒曼的前一天宣布了这笔军售。穆罕默德·本·萨勒曼是沙特事实上的领导人。 这笔军售现在已进入更深入阶段，而国防情报局较新的报告提出了更为强烈的担忧，包括技术方面的担忧。国务院已于6月将包括48架战机和一台备用发动机的拟议销售方案送交两个国会委员会，以寻求非正式批准。一些议员和国会工作人员一直就情报机构提出的担忧向政府施压。 由于间谍和军事事务的敏感性，这些美国官员在谈及情报官员的担忧时要求匿名。 美国国务院、五角大楼和沙特驻华盛顿大使馆拒绝置评。白宫和中国大使馆没有回应置评请求。 在特朗普第一个任期内，美国情报机构也曾在内部提出类似担忧。当时，特朗普于2020年同意向阿拉伯联合酋长国出售F-35战机，作为阿联酋与以色列 关系正常化 协议的一部分。 F-35战机由洛克希德·马丁公司生产，从生产到交付需要数年时间。因此，拜登政府在战机生产和交付之前很久就决定对这笔军售进行审查。当时，由于阿联酋正在 加强与中国在军事、情报和技术领域的联系 ，美国情报机构也提出了同样的问题。随后，美国官员 终止了这一军售进程 。 穆罕默德王储一直在努力提升沙特的军事实力。他曾在也门对胡塞武装发动一场灾难性的七年战争，沙特领导的部队在那场战争中使用美国炸弹 杀害平民 。在当前 美国和以色列对伊朗发动的战争 中，沙特军队也 未能阻止 来自伊朗的袭击，而沙特与伊朗支持的胡塞武装已 重新开始交战 。 穆罕默德王储长期以来一直寻求从美国购买F-35战斗机，特朗普最终于去年11月同意了这一要求。沙特和美国已经进行了数十年的军事合作，而沙特也是美国武器和防务装备的最大买家。但沙特同时也从中国购买弹道导弹，中国军方还在帮助沙特学习制造弹道导弹、建立生产设施以及改进导弹作战能力。 民主党议员曾于2022年6月 致信 拜登总统，阐述他们对这一项目的担忧。 一名美国官员说，五角大楼近期的情报报告指出，能进入存放F-35技术的设施的只有只有沙特和美国的军官及承包商。五角大楼官员尤其担心如何保护F-35先进的雷达和监视技术。 情报分析人士在报告中质疑沙特是否会进一步同意限制与中国军事和情报人员及相关实体的接触。 报告还质疑沙特官员是否会同意将华为和中兴这两家知名中国科技公司的设备从电信和路由器基础设施以及国防设施中移除。 一些以色列官员也对这笔军售表示担忧，就像特朗普当初提议向阿联酋出售F-35时一样。以色列是中东唯一拥有F-35战斗机的国家，近年来曾使用这些战机对伊朗发动空袭。自1973年阿以战争以来，美国政策制定者一直试图确保以色列在该地区保持国会所要求的“定性军事优势”。 历届美国政府都会通过一个高度机密、持续数月的审查程序，评估拟议中的中东地区武器销售是否符合这一要求。然而，特朗普第二届政府仍在推动向以色列 大规模军售 ，尽管美国政治光谱的各派都有人呼吁停止或大幅减少军事支持。 在过去的一些情况下，国务卿鲁比奥以地区紧急状态为由，绕过国会批准程序，加快向以色列运送武器。如果国会领导人不同意F-35战机销售，他可能会采取同样做法。 特朗普还同意 帮助沙特建立民用核项目 。该项目本身也引发了安全担忧，因为穆罕默德王储曾誓言，如果伊朗建造核武器，沙特也会这样做。

content: 纽约 — 中国国家主席习近平即将访美之际，一批纽约藏人及支持者9月17日傍晚从联合国总部外出发，展开为期六天，约200英里的“独立徒步”， 一路走向首都华盛顿，表达对习近平来访的“不欢迎”。 这次徒步活动也延续了今年7月在联合国总部外自焚身亡的藏人活动人士洛嘎让赞(Lobga Rangzen)的诉求。纽约学生卡玛益西(Karma Yeshi)参加了这次独立徒步。她说，“其实我认识他很久了…从我从印度来到这里以后就认识他了…” 19岁的卡玛认识洛嘎让赞有10年之久，一提到他还是会忍不住落泪。卡玛说，“我们经常一起吃饭，跳舞。他(洛嘎让赞)总是帮助大家， 他会接我，送我回家，也总会跟我谈西藏的问题。” 今年7月1日，中国开始实施《民族团结进步促进法》。 隔天下午5点49分，洛嘎让赞在纽约联合国总部外自焚身亡。他长期参与西藏独立运动，曾担任西藏国民大会党纽约、新泽西分会主席。两个多月后，20名徒步者选择从同一地点， 在同一时刻启程。卡玛和她的母亲也在其中。 这次徒步行动的主要目的之一，就是抗议即将访美的中国国家主席习近平。 纽约藏人启动六天、200英里赴华盛顿徒步抗议 西藏国民大会党纽约、新泽西分会主席迪吉次仁(Dickyi Tsering)说, “习近平是一个独裁者…西藏正在发生的事情，都与他有关，现在‘蛇头’来到了这里，我们不能就这样让他来。我们必须用自己的方式表达抗议。” 迪吉次仁希望特朗普总统和习近平会面时，能提出西藏和人权问题。她说，“这次徒步是为了让人们看到这些苦难，看到西藏的孩子正在经历什么，有殖民式的寄宿学校，我们的语言正在被强行消除，以及反对《民族团结进步促进法》。” 9月17日晚上，徒步者们从联合国总部出发走到林肯隧道。9月18日(星期五)早上6点，队伍从费城独立大厅继续出发， 沿途向路人散发介绍西藏和他们诉求的资料，预计23日抵达华盛顿。多数参与者都是第一次进行这样的长距离徒步。 纽约藏人启动六天、200英里赴华盛顿徒步抗议 纽约居民洛桑次旦(Lobsang Tseten)说，“作为一个流亡藏人，即使生活在美国，我也看到我的父母，祖父母一路的挣扎，我已经是第三代藏人了，我觉得每一个藏人都应该为西藏发声。” 队伍里也有非藏人，包括来自俄罗斯南部卡尔梅克共和国的纽约佛教徒鲍尔·呼尔哈齐耶夫。他说，“我们每天都祈祷，每天都为藏人，为西藏祈祷。” 六天，200英里之后，他们计划在24日走完最后一段，从华盛顿的中国驻美国大使馆走到白宫。

title: 众院通过俄伊制裁法案，最高100%二级关税授权，中国或首当其冲
summary: 美国国会众议院2026年9月16日以262票对159票通过了已故共和党籍联邦参议员林赛·格雷厄姆(Lindsey Graham)的制裁俄罗斯法案，并将其送交总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)签署。 华盛顿 — 美国国会众议院星期三(9月16日)通过一项大规模对俄制裁法案，赋予特朗普总统一项新的经济施压工具：对继续大量购买俄罗斯石油和天然气的国家输美商品征收最高100%的额外关税。 美国国会众议院星期三以262票对159票通过了这项名为《2026年林赛·格雷厄姆制裁
content: 美国国会众议院2026年9月16日以262票对159票通过了已故共和党籍联邦参议员林赛·格雷厄姆(Lindsey Graham)的制裁俄罗斯法案，并将其送交总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)签署。 华盛顿 — 美国国会众议院星期三(9月16日)通过一项大规模对俄制裁法案，赋予特朗普总统一项新的经济施压工具：对继续大量购买俄罗斯石油和天然气的国家输美商品征收最高100%的额外关税。 美国国会众议院星期三以262票对159票通过了这项名为《2026年林赛·格雷厄姆制裁俄罗斯和伊朗法》(Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026)的 法案 。由于参议院8月已经以86票对11票通过相同文本，法案现已送交白宫。唐纳德·特朗普(Donld Trump)总统此前表示支持这项立法，并预计将签署成法。 这项法案的主要目标是进一步压缩俄罗斯通过能源出口获得的财政收入。除了扩大对俄罗斯政府官员、金融机构、能源与国防部门以及用于规避制裁的“影子船队”的制裁之外，其中最受关注的一项条款，是允许对俄罗斯能源主要购买国实施范围广泛的所谓“二级关税”。 中国和印度目前被普遍视为这一规定最直接的潜在对象。中国研究机构数据显示，中国今年8月仍是俄罗斯化石燃料最大的海外买家，占俄罗斯前五大买家能源出口收入的51%。 什么是“二级关税”？ 传统制裁通常直接针对俄罗斯企业、银行或个人，而这项法案进一步瞄准与俄罗斯做生意的第三国。 法案规定，在成为法律30天后，如果一个国家继续“明知”购买俄罗斯原产石油或天然气，同时属于此前12个月俄罗斯石油或天然气进口量最大的五个国家之一，美国总统必须提高该国商品进入美国时的关税，税率最高可以达到100%。法案也涵盖被认定为协助俄罗斯规避石油制裁最严重的五个国家。 法案文字明确规定，如果一个国家符合条件，额外关税将适用于“从该国进口美国的所有商品”，并且是在其他已经存在的关税、反倾销税、301关税或232关税之上额外征收。 这意味着，如果中国最终被认定符合条件，受影响的理论范围可以覆盖几乎全部中国输美商品，而不仅限于能源或与俄罗斯交易直接相关的产品。 虽然中国并没有在法律文本中被“自动制裁”，但从当前贸易情况看，中国很可能成为行政部门首先需要评估的国家之一。 独立研究机构能源与清洁空气研究中心(CREA)的数据显示，今年8月中国是俄罗斯最大的化石燃料买家，对俄能源采购约84亿欧元，其中约58亿欧元为原油。 “该法案传递了美国团结的强烈信号，并为政府提供了所有必要手段，以帮助将这场战争引向公正的结局。我们很自豪能将该法案提交给总统签署，”众议院议长迈克·约翰逊(Mike Johnson)在法案通过后发表的声明中表示。 众议院版的法案发起人之一、德克萨斯州共和党籍联邦众议员迈克尔·麦考尔(Michael McCaul)对记者说，“制裁很好，但它们是可以被规避的。而关税就不能被规避。所以这就是关税的威力。而头号违规者是中国。如果我们既对中国实施制裁又征收关税，中国就可以对普京施加压力，让他坐到谈判桌上。” “最高100%”并不等于一定征100% 法案给予总统和美国贸易代表相当大的执行空间。 法律规定，初始税率可以在最高100%的范围内设定。之后，美国贸易代表可以根据有关国家是扩大还是减少俄罗斯能源采购，对税率进行调整。 如果一个国家显著减少俄罗斯能源采购，特朗普政府可以降低税率；如果其采购增加，行政部门也可以提高税率。 此外，总统可以基于美国国家利益给予豁免，但必须事先向国会提交书面证明，并解释为何豁免符合美国国家利益。 这一设计意味着，这项法案既是一套制裁机制，也给总统留下了相当大的外交谈判空间。 这导致部分民主党人担心法案将给予特朗普总统更宽松的施加关税权力。仅有58名民主党人和一名独立议员对法案投下赞成票。 法案通过后，民主党众议员斯坦尼·霍耶(Steny Hoyer)在回答记者有关他花了八个小时打电话，说服民主党同僚投赞成票的提问时说，“我向他们解释了为什么我认为明确表态支持乌克兰、支持制裁，并明确指出制裁基本上仅限于九个国家，这一点至关重要。我们民主党人担心总统会利用这项授权，将其使用到许多其他国家。” 法案通过时机受关注 法案通过的时机尤其受到关注。特朗普总统预计9月24日在华盛顿与中国国家主席习近平举行峰会。俄罗斯能源、伊朗以及美中经贸关系都可能成为双方讨论议题。 如果特朗普总统将法案签署，白宫将首次拥有一项经国会明确授权、可以直接把中国对俄能源采购与几乎全部中国输美商品关税挂钩的法律工具。 中国外交部发言人郭嘉昆星期四在例行记者会上表示，中国一贯反对没有国际法依据、没有经过联合国安理会授权的“非法单边制裁和长臂管辖”。 俄罗斯2022年全面入侵乌克兰后，欧美国家大幅减少购买俄罗斯石油，中国和印度随后成为俄罗斯能源出口最重要的市场之一。 今年8月，中国仍占俄罗斯前五大化石燃料买家所贡献收入的一半以上。俄罗斯原油也在中国进口能源结构中占据重要地位。 下一步是什么？ 特朗普总统已经表示他将签署这项法案。一旦签署，根据法案文本，行政部门将在30天内开始确定哪些国家符合俄罗斯石油、天然气主要进口国或制裁规避协助国的标准，并决定初始关税税率。随后，美国贸易代表必须至少每180天重新评估俄罗斯能源主要进口国。 在实际加征关税至少10天前，白宫或美国贸易代表还必须向国会提交书面说明，解释选择该国以及确定具体税率的依据。 乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基(Volodymyr Zelenskyy)在X上发贴，对法案最终获得通过表示感谢。 他随后在另一条 贴文 中点名批评中国未能向俄罗斯施压，协助结束战争。“我没看到中国在推动俄罗斯停止战争。我从来没看到过，”他写道，“中国可以找到办法让普京走向谈判。我肯定，但他们没这么做。如果你能做到却没有做，那算支持吗？”

title: Japan Opens The Door To Acquiring Nuclear-Powered Submarines
summary: Japan has said it is keeping the door open to acquiring nuclear-powered submarines , a potentially major shift for a country whose submarine force has historically relied exclusively on conventional propulsion. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koi
content: Japan has said it is keeping the door open to acquiring nuclear-powered submarines , a potentially major shift for a country whose submarine force has historically relied exclusively on conventional propulsion. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi confirmed recently that Tokyo is not ruling out nuclear-powered submarines as it considers the future requirements of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (JMSDF). Should Japan ultimately pursue the capability, it would join an exclusive group of nations operating nuclear-powered submarines. China, France, India, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States are currently the only countries with nuclear-powered submarines in active service. Brazil is already working to join the club, while Australian and South Korean nuclear-powered submarine plans are somewhat longer-term . A submarine of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force surfaces during a naval review off Sagami Bay, Japan. Photo by Koichi Kamoshida/Getty Images Japan’s submarine fleet is already regarded as among the most capable conventionally powered forces, and is very much at the forefront of advanced naval propulsion technologies . Even with that considerable expertise, however, developing and sustaining a nuclear propulsion capability would represent a huge challenge, requiring expertise and infrastructure far beyond those needed to build Japan’s existing conventionally powered submarines. Koizumi’s comments do not represent a decision to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, nor do they indicate that Japan has begun a procurement program. They do, however, mark a significant evolution in the country’s public debate over submarine propulsion and point to a growing willingness within the Japanese defense establishment to consider capabilities that were previously largely outside the mainstream of defense planning. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth hosts a bilateral meeting with Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjirō Koizumi at the Pentagon, Washington, D.C., Jan. 15, 2026. (DoW photo by U.S. Navy Petty Officer 1st Class Alexander Kubitza) Currently, Japan operates one of the world’s most capable conventional submarine fleets, centered on increasingly sophisticated diesel-electric boats equipped with air-independent propulsion and advanced lithium-ion batteries . These submarines are well suited to operations around Japan and the country’s surrounding waters. The JMSDF currently operates 22 conventionally powered submarines, maintaining the force structure established in the 2010s while progressively replacing older boats with the more capable Taigei class . Five Taigei class submarines are now in JMSDF service, with additional boats in the pipeline. The first-of-class Taigei was launched on October 14, 2020, at the Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) shipyard in the city of Kobe, in the western prefecture of Hyogo. Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Nuclear propulsion, however, would offer substantially greater endurance and sustained underwater speed, allowing Japanese submarines to conduct longer-range operations across the broader Western Pacific with minimal support. This is a requirement that is becoming increasingly relevant as Tokyo’s strategic focus expands beyond its immediate maritime approaches. China’s rapidly expanding naval force , including its growing submarine fleet and increasingly distant maritime operations , is forcing Tokyo to consider how it would monitor and potentially counter Chinese forces farther from the Japanese archipelago. A nuclear-powered attack submarine could remain submerged for extended periods without the endurance limitations imposed by conventional propulsion, making it particularly useful for long-range surveillance, tracking, and sea-denial missions. Japan’s debate is also unfolding alongside a significant development in neighboring South Korea. Seoul has confirmed plans to develop a new class of nuclear-powered submarines , a move that could add further momentum to an emerging undersea competition in Northeast Asia. South Korea’s decision is particularly relevant to Tokyo because it demonstrates that nuclear propulsion is no longer merely a theoretical capability for U.S. allies in the region. While the missions and strategic priorities of the Japanese and South Korean navies are different, both countries face the challenge of operating in waters increasingly contested by China and North Korea. A South Korean Ministry of Defense rendering shows how the nuclear-powered Jang Bogo N Project boats may look.  MND The development could also create new opportunities for Japan to work more closely with Australia and the other AUKUS partners. Australia is in the process of acquiring its own conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarine capability under AUKUS Pillar I, with U.S. and U.K. nuclear-powered submarines also scheduled to operate from Australia . Japan has separately been identified as a potential partner for AUKUS Pillar II, which covers advanced capabilities and technology cooperation. A Japanese decision to pursue SSNs could eventually create a much deeper basis for cooperation with Australia, including submarine interoperability, undersea warfare, workforce and technical expertise, infrastructure, sustainment, and potentially aspects of the industrial base. Analysts have already examined how Japan could fit into the wider AUKUS submarine ecosystem as Australia’s nuclear-submarine program develops. Concept art of the submerged  SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered attack submarine. U.K. Ministry of Defense illustration A Japanese nuclear-powered submarine with a robust capacity to launch land attack cruise missiles would also be a powerful component in the country’s emerging “counterstrike” posture , which is increasingly centered on acquiring the ability to strike targets at longer ranges. Japan has already begun deploying domestically developed long-range missile systems, including the Upgraded Type 12 surface-to-ship missile , while also acquiring the U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missile . Launch of the first  Tomahawk missile from the  Kongō   class Aegis destroyer   Chōkai   at an undisclosed location in the Pacific.  Japan Ministry of Defense An SSN would potentially add a highly survivable, mobile platform to this emerging strike architecture, allowing Japan to position long-range weapons farther from its home territory and complicating an adversary’s efforts to locate and neutralize them. That could be particularly valuable in a conflict in which Japanese air bases, missile batteries, and other fixed infrastructure were under attack. The potential SSN requirement also fits with Japan’s expanding expeditionary ambitions. As the JMSDF converts its Izumo class helicopter destroyers to operate F-35B fighters , giving Japan a more credible carrier aviation capability , nuclear-powered attack submarines could provide a valuable escort for these increasingly important surface groups. Their speed, endurance, and ability to remain submerged for extended periods makes SSNs particularly well suited to accompanying carrier forces on longer-range deployments and supporting contingencies farther from Japanese waters. Looking at the bigger picture, it is highly significant that nuclear propulsion was effectively excluded from Japan’s conventional defense debate for decades. More recently, however, Japanese defense officials and policymakers have begun examining whether future submarines will require a different propulsion system. The issue is now one that can be discussed openly at the ministerial level. Nevertheless, pursuing a nuclear-powered submarine program would come with huge challenges. The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Sōryū class submarine Hakuryū arrives at the submarine piers of Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Steven Khor/Released Building and operating nuclear-powered submarines would require Japan to establish an entirely different industrial, regulatory, and training infrastructure. The vessels would also be considerably more expensive and complex to build and operate than Japan’s existing conventionally powered submarines. Tokyo would have to resolve questions involving nuclear regulation, reactor technology, maintenance facilities, crew training, and the handling of nuclear material. There would also be a significant political dimension. Although naval nuclear propulsion is fundamentally different from possessing nuclear weapons, any move in that direction would inevitably receive scrutiny in a country whose postwar security policy has been shaped by its experience with nuclear weapons and its longstanding non-nuclear principles . For those reasons, Koizumi’s statement should be viewed less as an announcement of a Japanese nuclear-submarine program than as evidence that the political barrier to discussing such a program is falling. The Japanese Oyashio class submarine Yaeshio transits the Philippine Sea during Exercise Pacific Vanguard 23. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Santiago Navarro The next question is whether the Japanese government will move from keeping the option open to actually studying a nuclear-powered submarine design, propulsion technology, and acquisition pathway in detail. If it does, the consequences could extend well beyond Japan’s submarine fleet. A Japanese nuclear-powered submarine capability would represent a major enhancement of Tokyo’s ability to operate across the Western Pacific and could alter the undersea balance between Japan, China, and the United States’ other regional allies. At the very least, the idea is one that is now part of wider discussions at the highest levels. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Japan Opens The Door To Acquiring Nuclear-Powered Submarines appeared first on TWZ .

title: Hyrox失禁风波：澳洲选手道歉、主办方承诺退款
summary: 图像来源，Getty Images 图像加注文字，乔安娜·维特日克（Joanna Wietrzyk）公开道歉 * * Author, 李澄欣 * Role, BBC中文记者 * Published 3 小时前 * 阅读时间: 3 分钟 澳洲运动员乔安娜·维特日克（Joanna Wietrzyk）日前在Hyrox北京站赛事失禁后继续比赛，并称[“赢了就是应了”](https://bbc.com/zhongwen/articles/c74e1wv1xkzo/trad)，引发各界批
content:
图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，乔安娜·维特日克（Joanna Wietrzyk）公开道歉

*       *   Author, 李澄欣
    *   Role, BBC中文记者

*   Published 3 小时前

*   阅读时间: 3 分钟

澳洲运动员乔安娜·维特日克（Joanna Wietrzyk）日前在Hyrox北京站赛事失禁后继续比赛，并称[“赢了就是应了”](https://bbc.com/zhongwen/articles/c74e1wv1xkzo/trad)，引发各界批评。

舆论发酵数天后，她公开向中国人、其他参赛者、观众及Hyrox主办单位致歉，并决定放弃该场比赛的积分。

此前，Hyrox共同创办人莫里茨·菲尔斯特（Moritz Fürste）也为事件道歉，主办方宣布向当天受影响选手全额退款。

Hyrox已更新赛例，明文规定若参赛者的“血液、呕吐物、尿液或粪便”构成健康风险，可被要求退赛。

图像来源，Instagram

图像加注文字，乔安娜·维特日克（Joanna Wietrzyk）发表道歉声明

## “人生并不只有比赛这件事”

乔安娜·维特日克周四（9月17日）在Instagram发[声明](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdYy-D9iEbw/)表示，比赛开始时感觉完全健康、身体状况良好，没预料到会出现任何不适。

“回想起来，我后悔当时没有选择退出赛道。我明白自己应该作出不同的决定。我为自己选择继续比赛的决定负责，并对由此造成的不适及困扰，深感抱歉。”

她说，正从这次经历中汲取教训，包括提醒自己“人生并不只有比赛这件事，以及要懂得在适当时候选择退下来”；经过反思后，决定“追溯性退出这场赛事”（retroactively withdraw from the race）及放弃所赢得的积分。

Hyrox是一个室内体能耐力赛，包含八个关卡，包括滑雪机、推雪橇、拉雪橇、波比蛙跳、划船机、农夫走路、沙袋弓箭步和药球掷扔，每个关卡皆搭配一公里的跑步组合而成。

Joanna Wietrzyk上周六（12日）在北京赛事期间怀疑失禁，排泄物沾染赛道和共用器材，但仍继续作赛并最终夺冠，引发公共卫生争议。

赛后，她在Instagram发布自拍照称“拼尽全力或打包回家……赢了就是赢了（Go hard or go home … a win is a win.）”。她其后删除有关动态，社交媒体帐号亦禁止留言。

图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，Hyrox北京站赛事

## 全额退款、更新赛例

失禁事件发生后，大量相关图片、影片在网上流传，引发广泛讨论。

Hyrox周一（14日）在最初的声明中，赞扬该选手“将自己推向极限”，又指网上出现暴力威胁或鼓励伤害运动员的言论，警告会永久禁止发布这类言论的人参加所有Hyrox赛事。

有关声明引发大量质疑，认为主办方的解释，是把顶尖选手和大众参赛者之间划分了双重标准，优待运动表现比较好的人。也有人指出，Hyrox明文禁止选手在赛道上吐痰、擤鼻涕或丢垃圾，却允许失禁选手继续作赛。

在批评声浪之下，Hyrox共同创办人莫里茨·菲尔斯特（Moritz Fürste）当晚道歉，承认大会在比赛期间未有即时介入是一个错误，强调会改善赛事流程和规则手册。

Hyrox中国团队周三（16日）进一步向受影响参赛者发送致歉声明邮件，承诺全额退款。

目前，Hyrox已更新全球赛例，规定若参赛者的“血液、呕吐物、尿液或粪便”对其本人或其他参赛者构成健康或污染风险，可被要求退赛。

图像来源，Hyrox

图像加注文字，Hyrox已更新赛例，明文规定若参赛者的“血液、呕吐物、尿液或粪便”构成健康风险，可被要求退赛。

Hyrox是近年新兴的健身竞赛品牌，2017年创立后在全球快速扩张。2025至2026赛季扩展至逾100场赛事，吸引超过140万名参赛者及逾150万名观众。

这个热潮也席卷中国，Hyrox与中国全国600多间健身房展开长期合作。

国立台湾体育运动大学副教授黄世杰曾对BBC中文分析，Hyrox在不到十年间迅速完成全球化、媒体化与高度商业化，“商业成熟得太快，运动制度与文化还来不及跟上”。

content:
## “运动员无法伸直双腿睡觉”：日本亚运为何爆发住宿争议？

图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，日本亚洲运动会将于周六开幕，但由于赛程庞大，已有数个项目抢先开始。图为中国对菲律宾女子排球B组预赛，菲律宾队球员正在庆祝得分。

*       *   Author, 郭悠（Koh Ewe）

*   Published 2026年9月18日早上8点42分

最近更新： 2 小时前
*   阅读时间: 2 分钟

日本亚洲运动会将于周六（9月19日）开幕，住宿问题成为外界激烈批评的焦点。

其中，为数千名运动员而设的木制货柜屋，赛前被指漏水和床舖太小。

“身高超过两米（6呎7吋）的运动员，甚至无法在床上把腿伸直，这实在不合理。”韩国篮球协会副会长郑载龙（音译Jung Jae-yong）说。

他向法新社形容，这些住宿设施是“历来最差的”。

本届赛事于名古屋市及爱知县举行，超过1.7万名运动员及官员出席，比原先预计的人数多了2000人，过去数周以来外界都担心床位不足。

图像来源，AFP via Getty Images

图像加注文字，这些货柜屋预计将在日本举行的亚洲运动会期间容纳约2,000名运动员。

## 漏水的货柜屋

木制货柜屋将容纳约2000人，并设计为日后可重复用作灾害疏散设施，但一直饱受批评。

韩国篮球队一名成员上传影片，显示房间内有水管漏水及地面积水，并附上文字：“请帮帮我。”

上周名古屋遭遇破纪录降雨并引发大范围水灾后，入住货柜屋的运动员亦曾短暂疏散。一些比赛场馆亦传出漏水情况。

篮球官员郑载龙向法新社表示，其他参赛国家代表亦有相同住宿方面的忧虑。

印度当局甚至搭建了这些货柜屋的复制版本，让本国运动员预先适应相关住宿环境。

亚运住宿事务负责人松雄裕太（Yuta Matsuo）向路透社表示，主办方“充分了解各代表团提出的不满及忧虑”，强调正“采取具体措施改善运动员的住宿环境”。

图像来源，AFP via Getty Images

图像加注文字，除了货柜屋之外，数千名运动员将入住这艘意大利邮轮。

有别于奥运会通常设有专属选手村，亚运的主办单位选择以临时住宿设施安置参赛者。

除货柜屋外，另有4000至5000名参赛者将入住一艘意大利邮轮。该邮轮已于周二停靠名古屋，其余与会人士则将入住酒店。

大会最初预计，将有1.5万名运动员及官员参加本届亚运会。但亚洲奥林匹克理事会于8月中旬表示，在新增结合足球与桌球元素的桌式足球（teqball）及板式网球（padel）项目后，参与人数将接近1.7万人。

亚运组委会主席兼爱知县知事大村秀章（Hideaki Omura）此前表示，当局原本只为1.5万人编列预算，对于新增运动员“既没有足够人力，也没有足够预算作出必要安排”。

他说：“根本没有地方让他们住宿。如果他们仍希望前来，就必须自行安排。”

不过，上月主办方与亚洲奥林匹克理事会表示，所有于7月截止日期前完成报名的“超过1.7万名”运动员及官员，均已获提供“符合亚运标准的住宿安排”。

声明表示：“所有最后准备工作均按计划进行，且进展顺利。本届亚运会有望成为数十年来最精彩的一届。”

菲律宾奥林匹克委员会主席托伦蒂诺（Abraham Tolentino）向法新社表示，虽然所有菲律宾运动员都已获安排床位，但部分官员及教练则入住“不同的酒店和Airbnb”。

本届亚洲运动会将于周六（9月19日）正式揭幕，并于10月4日闭幕。目前，篮球及足球赛事已经展开。

**我们使用了人工智慧协助翻译这篇文章，它的原文是英文。在发布之前，BBC记者检查了翻译的内容。**

title: US hands over 64 artefacts to China in diplomatic push before leaders’ meeting
summary: At the handover ceremony at the Chinese embassy in Washington on Wednesday, China received 58 pieces of cultural relics and palaeontological fossils from the Cultural Property, Art and Antiquities programme of US Homeland Security Investiga
content:
At the handover ceremony at the Chinese embassy in Washington on Wednesday, China received 58 pieces of cultural relics and palaeontological fossils from the Cultural Property, Art and Antiquities programme of US Homeland Security Investigations.

A further six items were returned a day later by the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office in New York.

Southern China’s biggest natural history museum opens in Shenzhen

“The repatriation marks the latest step to implement the common understandings reached by the two presidents in their meetings in Beijing, and also demonstrates the broad prospects of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability,” said Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for China’s foreign ministry, at a briefing on Friday.

“China and the US should go in the same direction in the spirit of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit so as to accomplish more great and concrete things for the good of our two countries and peoples.”

According to the Chinese embassy in Washington, the returned items included a Bodhisattva statue from the [Tianlong Mountain Grottoes](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3284661/how-passion-and-tech-resurrected-chinas-headless-statues-and-unearthed-historic-wrongs?module=inline&pgtype=article) in the northern province of Shanxi, which was looted and taken overseas more than a century ago.

[Xie Feng](https://www.scmp.com/topics/xie-feng?module=inline&pgtype=article), China’s ambassador to the US, said at the ceremony that the repatriation reflected both sides’ responsibility for history and showed that China-US cooperation based on mutual respect and benefit could deliver many “major, practical and meaningful achievements”.

The handover occurred just days before Xi’s scheduled visit to Washington next week. It is a reciprocal trip following US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, where the two leaders agreed on a new positioning for China-US relations, building a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability.

“This repatriation stands as a tangible outcome of both sides implementing this new positioning,” Xie said.

A returned paleontological fossil is pictured at the Chinese embassy in Washington on September 9. Photo: Xinhua

He said the returned cultural relics – ranging from pottery figurines and stone sculptures to dinosaur and fish fossils, all of which were illicitly trafficked into the US before being seized by US law enforcement – carried “high historical, cultural and scientific value”.

He added that cultural heritage preservation had become a fruitful area of Sino-American cooperation.

China and the US signed their first intergovernmental memorandum of understanding to prevent the illegal entry of Chinese cultural artefacts into the US in 2009. It has since been renewed in 2014, 2019 and 2024.

Guo said the memorandum had so far allowed the return of more than 700 artefacts from the US.

The largest single repatriation of Chinese cultural relics from the US occurred in 2019, with 361 items retrieved.

According to the China Cultural Relics Academy, more than 10 million Chinese cultural artefacts have been lost overseas since the Opium Wars in the mid-19th century, mostly because of wartime looting and illegal trafficking.

title: Vietnam attends Mekong-Lancang forum on combating fake news in Cambodia
summary: Friday, 13:12, 18/09/2026 ## Vietnam attended a media forum and award ceremony for a 2026 anti-fake news contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on September 17, highlighting the importance of information integrity in the Mekong-Lancang region. Pa
content:
Friday, 13:12, 18/09/2026

## Vietnam attended a media forum and award ceremony for a 2026 anti-fake news contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on September 17, highlighting the importance of information integrity in the Mekong-Lancang region.

Participants at the opening ceremony of the forum

The forum, themed "Combating Fake News and Promoting Information Integrity in the Mekong-Lancang Region," brought together Cambodian Minister of Information Neth Pheaktra, Vietnamese Ambassador to Cambodia Nguyen Minh Vu, representatives of the embassies of China and ASEAN countries in Cambodia, and delegations from Mekong-Lancang Cooperation (MLC) member countries. The event also attracted media experts, reporters, journalists, and content creators. Organised by the Cambodian Ministry of Information in coordination with the Mekong-Lancang Cooperation Special Fund, the forum aimed to raise public awareness of the risks and consequences of fake news and irresponsible information sharing. It also provided a platform for participants to exchange experience in fact-checking and strengthen regional cooperation to curb the spread of misinformation.

Speaking at the event, Kan Pharidh, Secretary of State at the Cambodian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation and Chairman of the Cambodia’s National Secretariat for Mekong-Lancang Cooperation, noted that digital transformation and advances in artificial intelligence have created major opportunities while also increasing the risks posed by misinformation, disinformation, and deliberately distorted content.

If left unaddressed, these challenges could undermine public trust, damage the credibility of institutions, weaken social cohesion, and negatively affect peace, stability, and cooperation in the region, he said.

Kan Pharidh called for stronger joint efforts within the MLC framework to address the negative impacts of misleading information on regional development. He also stressed the importance of providing timely, reliable, and accurate information, highlighting the role of professional and responsible journalism in building public trust and promoting mutual understanding.

For his part, Minister Neth Pheaktra shared that combating fake news should go beyond correcting false information after it has spread. He called for the development of an information ecosystem that ensures access to reliable information, maintains high professional media standards, promotes effective public communication, and encourages responsible technology use and digital literacy.

He highlighted Cambodia’s ongoing efforts through the “No Fake News” campaign and initiatives promoting media and digital literacy, professional journalism, responsible content creation, and timely public communication.

Following discussions and experience-sharing sessions, the organisers presented the "Zero Fake News Media and Content Creator Awards" to five journalistic works that had made positive contributions to society.

# Yemen conflict displaces 112,000 people inside country, thousands flee to Djibouti, UN migration agency says

By [Olivia Le Poidevin](https://www.reuters.com/authors/olivia-le-poidevin/)

September 18, 2026 9:31 AM UTC Updated 2 hours ago

*
*
*

*
*
*
*
*

GENEVA, Sept 18 (Reuters) - At least 112,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen within the last two weeks as fighting continues along the country's west ​coast amid a renewed [conflict,](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-strike-saudi-targets-anew-talks-over-strait-hormuz-stall-2026-09-15/) while nearly 3,000 have fled by sea to ‌Djibouti, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure while advancing along Yemen's Red Sea coast towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ​key shipping route. Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air ​forces have bombarded Houthi targets.

The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/reuters-iran-briefing/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fmiddle-east%2Fyemen-conflict-displaces-112000-people-inside-country-thousands-flee-djibouti-un-2026-09-18%2F)

Nearly 3,000 people have crossed the Gulf of ⁠Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in less than a week as ​escalating violence have forced more families to flee, Sandrine Desamours, the representative for the UN’s ​refugee agency, UNHCR, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Djibouti.

The government of Djibouti is preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees - which will add acute pressure on the country’s health ​care and education services, she said.

Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Stringer [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/escaped-with-only-our-lives-yemenis-flee-houthi-clashes-to-overcrowded-displacement-camps/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMkdJTkFEWldGSA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

The UN International Organization for Migration said people are ​fleeing on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water. Most fleeing are Yemeni families ‌seeking ⁠refuge in Djibouti, but IOM is also beginning to see a small number of migrants, mainly from Ethiopia, heading in the same direction.

Additionally, authorities in Somaliland and Puntland have also reported increased arrivals from Yemen, including Yemeni refugees and Somali refugee returnees, though numbers ​remain in the hundreds ​for now, UNHCR ⁠said.

UN agencies described the latest fighting as being a crisis on top of multiple crises as the country’s health services and economy ​have been shattered amid a long [civil war](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/who-is-fighting-yemen-2026-09-10/) between forces of the ​internationally recognised, ⁠Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis created one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.

The Houthi advance along Yemen's Red Sea coast is bolstering Tehran’s hand in its conflict with the US, as the group tightens its ⁠control of ​the [Bab el-Mandeb Strait](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/why-is-bab-el-mandeb-strait-so-important-2026-09-10/), a strategic chokepoint for global ​oil and commodities shipping, more than six months after US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
