title: North Korea says US-led arms buildup justifies expanding nuclear force
summary: North Korea's Vice Defence Minister Kim Kang Il and other military officials attend a plenary session at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, China September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Florence Lo Florence Lo Reuters Sept 17 (Reuters) - North Kor
content:
North Korea's Vice Defence Minister Kim Kang Il and other military officials attend a plenary session at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, China September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Florence Lo  Florence Lo Reuters

Sept 17 (Reuters) - North Korea's vice defence minister said on Thursday that a growing U.S.-led military buildup and what he called an expanding nuclear alliance among Washington, Seoul and Tokyo justified Pyongyang's efforts to strengthen and expand its nuclear forces.

Speaking at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum, China's flagship international security conference, Vice Defence Minister Kim Kang Il said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was irreversible and pledged to continue expanding its nuclear arsenal.

"The ceaseless nuclear arms buildup of the enemy states fully justifies the building of a solid nuclear shield of the DPRK," Kim said, using the acronym for North Korea's formal name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

"As the enemy states' nuclear threat reaches the extreme level ... the DPRK will firmly defend the peace and stability in the Korean Peninsula and the region by ceaselessly expanding and strengthening its self-defensive nuclear deterrent."

Kim blamed tensions on the Korean Peninsula on what he called Washington's "invariable" hostile policy toward North Korea and accused the United States of turning trilateral cooperation with South Korea and Japan into a nuclear alliance.

He said North Korea's constitutional status as a nuclear weapons state was "the line of no retreat" and urged other countries to abandon what he called the "daydream" of denuclearisation.

Kim's appearance at the Xiangshan Forum marked a rare high-profile showing by North Korea at an international security gathering in recent years and came as Pyongyang seeks closer ties with Beijing amid tensions with Washington and its allies.

Asked about the possibility of a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, Kim said he was not in a position to discuss whether such a summit could take place.

Former U.S. Special Representative for North Korea Stephen Biegun said at the Korea Risk Group's West Coast Exchange conference on Thursday that North Korea's muted response to Trump's repeated claims of communication with Kim Jong Un suggested Pyongyang was "not closing the door" on potential future talks with Washington.

Biegun said it "would not be a surprise at all" if Trump were to propose a meeting with the North Korean leader following the APEC summit in China in November and that such a meeting could even take place in Pyongyang.

DENUCLEARISATION REJECTED

The North Korean official's remarks followed a statement on Thursday morning from Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of Kim Jong Un, rejecting renewed international calls for North Korea's denuclearisation following discussions at the annual meeting of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

In a statement carried by state media KCNA, she said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "absolute" and could not be reversed, dismissing repeated denuclearisation demands as annual "noise" and insisting Pyongyang's nuclear position had been permanently established "physically and legally".

Her comments echoed a separate statement on Wednesday by a North Korean defence ministry spokesman, who accused the United States and South Korea of escalating military confrontation through joint weapons-of-mass-destruction response planning and exercises.

The spokesman said recent U.S.-South Korean WMD response discussions amounted to an "open declaration of confrontation" and warned such actions could require Pyongyang to invoke provisions of its nuclear force policy law.

The statements appeared to form part of a broader messaging campaign by Pyongyang on its nuclear policy, according to Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies in Seoul.

The comments were aimed at cementing North Korea's claim that its nuclear status had reached an "irreversible stage", while creating justification for future military and nuclear activities in response to what it portrays as growing U.S. and South Korean pressure, Lim said.

(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim with additional reporting by Brenda GohEditing by Ed Davies)

title: Transcript of Stanton, McGovern, Khanna, Pelosi, and Moulton Opening Statements From Shadow Hearing on Human Rights in China Ahead of Xi’s Visit to Washington
summary: **WASHINGTON –**On Tuesday, the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party Minority and Congressional-Executive Commission on China Ranking Member Jim McGovern held a hearin
content:
**WASHINGTON –**On Tuesday, the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party Minority and Congressional-Executive Commission on China Ranking Member Jim McGovern held a hearing titled _The Void in China Policy: Why Human Rights Must Be on Trump’s Agenda with Xi at the White House._

The following witnesses provided testimony:

*   [**Tahir Imin**](https://democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/tahir-imin-testimony.pdf)**,**Founder and Director, Uyghur Post
*   [**Palden Gyal**](https://democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/statement-of-palden-gyal-president-of-international-tibetan-media-organization.pdf)**,**President, International Tibet Media Organization
*   [**Yaqiu Wang**](https://democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/statement-of-yaqiu-wang-joint-shadow-hearing-sep-15-2026-002.pdf)**,**Fellow at the Penn Project on the Future of U.S.-China Relations at the University of Pennsylvania
*   [**Jonathan Stivers**](https://democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/9.15.26-statement-of-jonathan-n-stivers.pdf)**,**U.S. Director, Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong; Commissioner, U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission’

Below is a transcript of opening statements delivered by Representative Greg Stanton, CECC Ranking Member McGovern, Ranking Member Khanna, Speaker Emerita Pelosi, and Representative Seth Moulton. A recording of the hearing can be found [here](https://www.youtube.com/live/TNK_FTr6STA?si=2OeaBqV7AqQudWxm&t=19 "(opens in a new window)").

[**Representative Greg Stanton**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oTMyyLRqCP8&list=PLXVS5RHTRsPc&index=8 "(opens in a new window)")

_First off, I want to acknowledge this gentleman sitting next to me. His entire career has been just one of the strongest voices in Congress, arguably in America, for human rights around the globe. So, thank you for your steadfast and consistent leadership._

_And the gentleman on my left, who is currently the ranking member of the Select Committee on China, because of the change in times and votes, he originally wasn't supposed to be here, but now he's able to be here. So, you get two of us from the Committee, so good to see you. Thank you, Ro Khanna._

_Thank you, Ranking Member McGovern, for your strong remarks and for co-chairing today's hearing on human rights abuses in the People's Republic of China._

_More than three and a half years ago, the Select Committee held its second hearing after being established. The second hearing of the Select Committee was particularly on the Chinese Communist Party's abuses of the Uyghur people._

_And today in 2026, that persecution continues._

_In January, a group of UN human rights experts alleged that the Chinese Communist Party continues to subject its Uyghur, Tibetan, and other minority populations to forced labor, using “coercive elements so severe that they may amount to enslavement and a crime against humanity.”_

_Beginning in 2017, the CCP arbitrarily detained more than a million ethnic Uyghurs and other Muslims in “re-education facilities,” which are just concentration camps._

_In these camps, parents are forcibly separated from their children. Children are sent to state-run boarding schools where they are systematically stripped of their native language, culture, and religious heritage._

_Adult detainees are subjected to political indoctrination, sexual violence, forced female sterilization and abortions, food deprivation, and other forms of torture. They are forced to renounce Islam as a condition for their release._

_This direction comes straight from the top. A CCP religious affairs official said in 2017 about the Uyghurs: the Chinese government will “break their lineage, break their roots, break their connections, and break their origins.”_

_Unfortunately, the CCP's severe repression is not isolated to Xinjiang._

_In 2024, 650,000 Tibetans were forced from the homes as part of a CCP program to systematically transfer what it called “rural surplus labor.”_

_Since 2000, it is estimated that almost 3.5 million Tibetans have been forced from their homes by the CCP, including through what are called "old village relocation" programs._

_In 1963, images of a Buddhist monk setting himself on fire to protest the South Vietnamese government shocked the conscience of our world. Since 2009, at least 170 Tibetans have self-immolated to protest the CCP's repression._

_We have to ask ourselves: where is the conscience of our world today?_

_Next week, President Trump will roll out the red carpet for Xi Jinping, honoring him with a state dinner at the White House. Unfortunately, the Trump administration has not shown much of a willingness to confront Xi about his horrific human rights abuses._

_This starts with President Trump himself, who, according to two former officials in the administration, encouraged Xi's creation of concentration camps in Xinjiang, telling Xi it was "exactly the right thing to do."_

_A senior Trump official who for a time was the acting president of the United States Institute of Peace blamed Uyghurs for the CCP's atrocities against them, saying that "the Chinese aren't genocidal, they just object to Uyghur-ness.”_

_Meanwhile, the Trump administration has attempted to pull the rug out from under human rights groups that are pushing back against the CCP’s abuses. They slashed funding and grants for human rights organizations, gutted the State Department's human rights bureaus, and tried to shutter groups that empower human rights defenders in China, like the National Endowment for Democracy and Radio Free Asia._

_President Trump has called Xi Jinping a “friend” and a “incredible man who has done amazing things.” It is unbefitting any leader of a great country to use words like that to describe someone who has oppressed the human rights and dignity of others._

_Standing up for the oppressed in the PRC, whether it be Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kongers, Mongolians, or Han Chinese has always been and must be a bipartisan issue._

_Chairman, Co-Chair, we have incredible witnesses today. People who have shown unbelievable courage. We are inspired by you, your actions, what you're doing to support the people you represent. It's incredible._

_I look forward to hearing from these incredible witnesses today on what more Congress can do and should do to hold the CCP accountable for its human rights abuses and stand up for all those who are oppressed by its autocratic rule._

[**Ranking Member McGovern**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TsdKC-KKzk4 "(opens in a new window)")

_We convene this hearing to shine a light on the severe violations of human rights by the government of China, and to assess our government's performance in holding it accountable._

_Human rights in China has long been an area of bipartisan concern and productivity here in the Congress._

_I think of Congresswoman Nancy Pelosi standing in Tiananmen Square with Republican and Democratic colleagues in 1991, bravely unfurling a banner to the victims of the massacre before being whisked away by police._

_I think of President George W. Bush and the bipartisan House and Senate leadership in 2007 presenting the Congressional Gold Medal to His Holiness the Dalai Lama._

_I think of Marco Rubio and myself as co-chairs of the CECC, working together to craft and pass the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act of 2021 into law._

_I think of institutions we created to monitor the Chinese government's behavior, the CECC, Select Committee, the U.S. Security and Economic Review Commission – and we welcome one of its commissioners today as a witness._

_There has been consensus that U.S. policy toward China must include a moral dimension; that we must speak out for the freedoms of those who cannot advocate for themselves. That we must deploy policy tools to press the Chinese government to respect human rights._

_That consensus, I fear, is disappearing – and here is why:_

_President Trump has removed human rights from U.S. foreign policy in favor of a transactional approach._

_President Trump carried no human rights agenda to Beijing, other than to ask to free two individuals – individuals we care deeply about – only one of which succeeded._

_Secretary Rubio decimated the State Department's Human Rights Bureau and cut grants to China human rights organizations._

_The Administration wants to eliminate Radio Free Asia and Voice of America, among the only sources of independent information for those living under the Chinese censorship regime._

_These actions take us backwards. They undermine so much that Republicans and Democrats have worked to build up over the years._

_But rather than defend the tools that helped us promote human rights in China, the Republican majority in Congress sat on their hands, and the numbers back this up._

_When Biden was president, the CECC averaged 15 hearings and 23 advocacy letters per Congress. With Trump as president, the CECC has scheduled only seven hearings and sent out only three letters._

_Between 2018 and 2024, Congress passed the Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act, the Tibetan Policy and Support Act, the Promoting a Resolution to the Tibet-China Dispute Act, the Uyghur Human Rights Policy Act, the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, the Hong Kong Autonomy Act, and the Protect Hong Kong Act – all bipartisan measures._

_This Congress has not sent one single China human rights bill to the president. Not one. And at the same time, our Republican colleagues are removing the words "human rights" and references to international human rights treaties from bills and resolutions._

_And here's an example: the House and the Senate passed resolutions calling for the release of Jimmy Lai. That’s good. But neither frames his case in human rights language. Neither mentions China's legally binding international human rights obligations that could be leveraged to secure his freedom._

_That omission does a disservice to the cause that Jimmy has gone to jail to defend._

_In my service on the CECC and as co-chair of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission, I have closely monitored human rights conditions in China. And make no mistake: the Chinese government remains one of the world's worst abusers of its own people._

_We have a moral obligation to speak out and to take action for those who suffer under this repression. But it is a real question whether the U.S. has the moral credibility to call on Chinese authorities to approve human rights._

_At the CECC, we report on how the Chinese government prosecutes journalists and political opponents of the of the ruling party, restricts freedom of expression and assembly, puts ethnic minorities in detention facilities, engages in arbitrary detention, and commits extrajudicial killings._

_But today, here in the United States, under the current administration, our own government, is committing each of the same violations, from the streets of Minneapolis to the Caribbean Sea. Our own government is murdering people in cold blood._

_Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and Chinese fled persecution in China and sought refuge in the United States. Now, our own government is detaining them and sending them to ICE facilities with the intention to deport them to a dark fate._

_I have publicly condemned this policy, but I don't know of a single one of my colleagues on the other side of the aisle who has had the courage to publicly criticize this president for this abuse, and I think that that's cowardly._

_The United States is rapidly forfeiting

**[1/3]**Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun delivers the keynote speech at the opening ceremony for the Beijing Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, China September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Florence Lo [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/beijing-xiangshan-forum/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMjBLTkE4SU5ESg%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

*   Summary
*   Companies

*   International tension meant world was at a 'fragile moment'
*   Forum comes amid regional tension, ahead of Xi's trip to US
*   No direct criticism of US and its allies
*   Sharp exchange between Iran and Saudi Arabian delegates

BEIJING, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Chinese Defence ​Minister Dong Jun urged nations on Wednesday to avoid provocative acts and curb the resurgence of regressive historical trends in ‌remarks likely to be taken as veiled criticism of Japan.

Dong's comments at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on security come at a time of roiling regional tension over China-claimed Taiwan and the disputed South China Sea waterway, as doubt grows over traditional U.S. security commitments to Asia.

Make sense of global markets with the Trading Day newsletter. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/trading-day/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fchina%2Fchina-defence-minister-urges-an-end-provocative-acts-open-security-forum-2026-09-16%2F)

Warning that the world had arrived at a "fragile moment", Dong called for a ​fresher, more equal approach to resolving international tension, but offered few specifics or direct criticism of rivals.

"We must bear in mind the ​lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against all latent manifestations of hegemony, militarism and historical revisionism," he said ⁠in an opening speech.

"We must not turn a blind eye or condone such behaviour. By rallying broad-based forces of justice, we must suppress the resurgence ​of historical dregs and prevent them from exploiting the situation to cause harm."

Ties between China and Japan plummeted last year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ​suggested a hypothetical Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger a Japanese military response.

That spurred Beijing to [repeatedly warn](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/taiwan-china-world-war-two-its-aftermath-2025-08-24/) that Japan was seeking a return to its militarist past, which included the Japanese occupation of northeast China's Manchuria in 1931 before a full war between the then-Republic of China and Japan.

Some 2,000 military officers, diplomats and academics from 100 countries are attending ​the three-day event set to run until Thursday, with delegates including some regional defence ministers, a senior Pentagon official, Russian academics and Taliban representatives.

## NO ​DIRECT CRITICISM OF U.S. OR REGIONAL ALLIES

As some analysts predicted, Dong steered clear of direct criticism of the United States or its regional allies, such as Japan, and appeared to ‌hew closely ⁠to long-held Chinese positions.

Dong urged efforts towards a peaceful, multipolar world marked by "partnership rather than alliance, win-win rather than zero sum".

"We must show no leniency towards provocative acts that seek to hijack the overall interests of countries in the region for the sake of personal gain or the interests of particular cliques, and we must work together to rein them in," he added.

The comments come a week before Chinese President [Xi](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/xi-jinping/)Jinping is expected to visit the United ​States for a summit with President [Donald ​Trump](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/donald-trump/).

[China](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/) views democratically governed [Taiwan](https://www.reuters.com/world/taiwan/) as ⁠its own territory and has ramped up military pressure around the island, including periodically staging war games. Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's claims of sovereignty.

A tightly scripted rival to the more prominent Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, which is widely seen ​as a more freewheeling affair, the forum comes at a time of China's expansion of military diplomacy. This often ​takes the form of [bilateral ⁠exercises](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-indonesia-navies-hold-drills-sensitive-waters-east-taiwan-2026-08-11/) that military attaches say are slowly growing in complexity.

One of the sharper exchanges took place when a Saudi Arabian think-tank researcher, Prince Turki Al-Faisal, shared a panel with a senior Iranian military officer, Mohammad Taghi Osanlou.

Osaulou said the U.S. was attempting to maintain its "unipolar hegmonic system" against the tide of history, ⁠and external forces ​were tearing apart Middle Eastern unity.

While also criticising the U.S. and Germany, Al-Faisal said ​Saudi Arabia's immediate concern was Iran's inability to respect the sovereignty of the Arab states "culminating in its aggressive and unlawful attacks on their territories and assets in the recent war."

She began her journalism career at Malaysia’s largest English-language newspaper and is an alumna of the Oxford Climate Journalism Network. She brings a cross-disciplinary lens to her coverage of policy and diplomacy.

content:
香港 —

澳门首宗国安法案件星期三(9月16日)开庭，闭门审理前民主派议员区锦新被控“颠覆国家政权”案。区锦新被捕一年至今音讯全无，家属也无法自行聘用律师。外界普遍认为，澳门当局以“官派律师”为其辩护，和所有中国大陆维权案类似，区锦新不可能得到公平的审讯。

区锦新在去年7月被捕前持续公开评论澳门当局的施政，并在“六四”后连续多年筹办悼念活动。

美国之音尝试联系他身在英国的女儿区翰怡，但一直未获回复。一名要求匿名的知情人士向美国之音透露，自区锦新被捕后，家属一直无法与他联系，也无法为他委托辩护律师。

**法院指派律师为区锦新辩护**

今年3月, 澳门通过法规，允许国安案件闭门审讯，并强制参与的律师要先通过审查。部分舆论形容，新法规似乎是为区锦新案“量身定制”。

今年7月, 区锦新案完成预审，法院以“颠覆国家政权”、“与澳门特别行政区以外的组织、团体或个人建立联系作出危害国家安全的行为”及“违反保密”三项控罪将其起诉. 其中“颠覆国家政权”最高可处10至25年监禁。

知情人士披露，家属曾先后尝试委托不同律师为区辩护，但最终这些律师都表示无法接案。

在日本的香港人权活动家潘嘉伟对美国之音表示，区锦新的遭遇与中国大陆的被捕异议人士非常相似。

潘嘉伟说：“我们看到它们(澳门当局)对待(区锦新)的手法非常恶劣，跟中国大陆的做法差不多，(甚至)可能更严重，一开始已采取秘密审讯，而且不让他自己聘请律师，由所谓的‘官派律师’替他辩护。这跟我们多年以来所跟进的所有中国大陆维权个案一样，没有可能有公平的审讯。”

英国港侨协会董事、前澳门社运人士周庭希表示，闭门审讯让外界无从获悉控罪的具体内容，只能依赖法院宣判后发出的公告，有理由相信，澳门当局刻意隐瞒区锦新涉案的事实根据。

周庭希说：“香港无论47人案也好，支联会案也好，苹果日报案也好，所谓控罪的事实(法院)审讯时都会‘摊开来’。而澳门的‘司警’国安部门却是相对神秘的组织。。。为什么区锦新案要闭门审讯呢？原因之一是，澳门当局知道，它们罗织的证据在外界看来并不确凿。”

**筹组“民联会”举办“六四”悼念活动**

68岁的区锦新原本是小学教师。1989年六四天安门事件后参与筹组“澳门民主发展联委会”(简称“民联会”)，提出“回应中国民主运动、推动澳门民主发展”,往后30年定期举办“六四”烛光晚会及相关声援活动。

2021年，澳门警方首次禁止举办“六四”烛光晚会。随着澳门修订《国安法》，“民联会”在翌年停止举办相关悼念活动，并于2023年5月解散。区锦新也曾担任澳门立法会议员长达20年，当时是议会内极少数民主派议员之一。2009年的一届立法会选举，周庭希曾加入区锦新的竞选团队。

周庭希说：“区锦新不畏强权，敢于批评有权有势的人。他热爱中国，而且是出于对中华民族的爱。他认为中国要有变化、改革，所以才会参与悼念‘六四’。”

人权活动家潘嘉伟相信，澳门当局把区锦新视为“眼中钉”与他的背景有关。

潘嘉伟说：“他(区锦新)是澳门非常有名的民主派人士。 (当局)以他作为目标就可以震慑公民社会人士不要继续办活动悼念‘六四’。澳门在《国安法》之下存在不少限制，但他还是很勇敢表达看法，批评澳门政府不同的政策。我担心他有可能被重判，沉重打击澳门公民社会。”

**欧盟将持续关注区锦新案**

近年来，澳门民主派人士和公民社会的生存空间不断缩小。区锦新是少数愿意公开接受外国传媒采访的当地政界人士。前澳门大学政治学者余永逸接受美国之音采访时表示，不排除此举为区锦新种下祸根。

余永逸说：“澳门本地媒体在评论时事的时候都比较亲政府。基本上澳门政府和北京掌控了本地的传媒，当局也会向社媒施压，要求它们删帖。只有外媒评论澳门时事，当局没有能力全面控制。区锦新(被捕前)跟外媒有很多联系，(向外媒)评论澳门问题。北京希望压制澳门居民，不让他们对外媒评论澳门的时事。”

外界形容，区锦新案作为国安案被安排闭门审理，无论在香港还是澳门都是首例。有法律界人士更把此案与香港的黎智英案比较，认为黎智英虽然经历长期关押，但他在羁押期间仍能与家人见面，并可自行聘用本地执业律师团队进行辩护。

学者余永逸不排除区锦新案的各种安排日后被香港司法当局复制的可能。

余永逸说：“闭门审讯早已在中国大陆出现。北京只是把它先引进到澳门，不排除将来香港也会有此安排，这将取决于北京认为有没有这样的需要。澳门不少法官与中国大陆都有紧密联系，甚至他们的学位也来自大陆，他们的意识形态可能与大陆较为接近。 ”

据了解，区锦新拥有葡萄牙国籍。去年欧盟曾谴责澳门当局把他逮捕。上周欧盟透过声明表示，区锦新接受正当法律程序的权利被剥夺，将持续向澳门当局提出关注。

title: Trump, in North Carolina, says Democrats are soft on crime and communism
summary: Republican Michael Whatley of North Carolina, a candidate for the U.S. Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, speaks during the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, U.S., September 9, 2026. REUTERS/Brian Snyder [Pur
content:
Republican Michael Whatley of North Carolina, a candidate for the U.S. Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, speaks during the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, U.S., September 9, 2026. REUTERS/Brian Snyder [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/republican-national-midterm-convention-in-dallas/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMlhGTkFQMUlHSQ%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

*   Summary

*   Campaign theme becoming clearer ahead of November midterm election
*   Trump seeks to rebuild his 2024 coalition in North Carolina
*   Affordability concerns threaten Republican support among unaffiliated voters

GASTONIA, North Carolina, Sept 16 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump campaigned in North Carolina on Wednesday for a Republican Senate candidate who is trailing his Democratic opponent, hammering exaggerated claims ​that Democrats favor crime and communism.

Those themes are likely to be central to Trump's promised series of appearances across the country to bolster his party ‌ahead of November 3 midterm elections. All 435 congressional seats and 34 of the Senate's 100 seats will be up for grabs, and Democrats are favored to regain control of the House while forecasts expect a close race for the Senate majority.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a "Real or Fake?" quiz in every edition. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/misinformation-monitor/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fus%2Ftrump-seeks-rebuild-support-among-2024-voters-north-carolina-2026-09-16%2F)

North Carolina was his first major campaign stop since the Republican Party's midterm convention last week, when he repeatedly sought to portray Democrats as extreme and out of ​touch on cultural matters while promoting his hard-line stance on immigration, a signature issue that twice helped vault him to the White House.

Trump sought to help Michael ​Whatley, who previously chaired the Republican National Committee, close a polling gap against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.

Trump predicted electoral victory, while ⁠misstating the character of the Democratic Party, which has seen the rise of a few democratic socialists but is far from communist.

"You're going to crush the communists, and that's ​what they are, they're communists ... We will not be a socialist nation. I was right. They're going for 'communist' nation," he said.

A screen showed photos of what he said were some of ​the 3,500 North Carolina inmates who were freed during Cooper's time as governor in a 2021 COVID-era settlement that reduced the state's prison population.

"Roy Cooper wants migrant criminals like these set loose on North Carolina streets with sanctuary city policies. Michael Whatley wants them executed, arrested, or deported," Trump told the partisan crowd during his one-hour appearance.

Trump remains a powerful force with the Republican base, but Whatley will also ​need to win over North Carolina's large bloc of swing and unaffiliated voters as Republicans confront rising concerns over affordability that have strained Trump's support among more moderate voters.

Trump ​repeated what he [told Republicans at the convention](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/five-big-takeaways-trumps-midterm-convention-2026-09-11/) in Dallas last week – to "pretend that I'm on the ballot," even though he is not seeking election.

## DEMOCRATS AHEAD IN POLLS

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the past ‌week [found Trump's approval ⁠rating](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-approval-up-record-low-outlook-sours-republicans-reutersipsos-poll-finds-2026-09-14/) at 35%, up from a record-low 33% in the previous poll. Democrats led Republicans 44% to 37% on the generic congressional ballot, the widest Democratic advantage in the Reuters/Ipsos series since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

Unaffiliated voters account for roughly 40% of North Carolina's registered electorate, making them the state's largest registration bloc.

Cooper led Whatley 49% to 38% among likely voters in a recent Elon University poll, while 54% of North Carolina voters in the survey disapproved of Trump's job performance and 31% approved.

"It's mathematically impossible ​to win the state without winning unaffiliated ​voters," said veteran Republican strategist Paul Shumaker, ⁠a former adviser to departing Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who opted against seeking re-election.

"We Republicans have to understand that we have to address the affordability issue, and we have to be able to put unaffiliated voters' minds at ease as it relates to the ​economy and affordability between now and November for the Senate race to remain in play."

Fuel prices have added to the affordability challenge. ​The national average for ⁠regular gasoline was $4.33 a gallon on Tuesday, while diesel reached a record $6.27, according to AAA.

Trump attempted to blame Democrats for America's affordability troubles.

"I got hit with this affordability word for a year and a half. And they're the ones that caused the affordability problem," Trump said, raising the issue of egg prices that became a concern during the 2021-2025 term of former President Joe ⁠Biden.

"We took care ​of the egg crisis. We took care of everything," Trump said, apparently betting he can sway voters with ​rhetoric.

"If they (Democrats) get in, this country will go into a massive depression," said Trump, who also promised once again to offer Americans a $5,000 rebate if the Republicans maintain control of Congress, although the proposal has failed to animate congressional ​Republicans who would need to approve the spending.

Reporting By Jarrett Renshaw in Charlotte, Additional reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, California; editing by Donna Bryson, Lincoln Feast and Stephen Coates

title: 美众院两委员会主席致函财长与国务卿，要求加强对与中共有关联的诈骗分子的制裁
summary: 众议院外交委员会主席布赖恩·马斯克(Brian Mast)与众议院中国问题特设委员会主席约翰·穆勒纳尔(John Moolenaar)星期二(9月15日)致函美国财政部长和国务卿，要求对与网络诈骗中心有关的外国人员实施更强有力的制裁。两位共和党众议员指出，这些坑害美国人的诈骗分子与中国共产党有关联。 这封信要求行政当局展开调查，并且在判定符合法律标准时，对与位于东南亚的网络诈骗中心有可信关联的外国人员实施制裁。 来自佛罗里达州的马斯特众议员和来自密歇根州的穆勒纳尔众议员在写给
content:
众议院外交委员会主席布赖恩·马斯克(Brian Mast)与众议院中国问题特设委员会主席约翰·穆勒纳尔(John Moolenaar)星期二(9月15日)致函美国财政部长和国务卿，要求对与网络诈骗中心有关的外国人员实施更强有力的制裁。两位共和党众议员指出，这些坑害美国人的诈骗分子与中国共产党有关联。

这封信要求行政当局展开调查，并且在判定符合法律标准时，对与位于东南亚的网络诈骗中心有可信关联的外国人员实施制裁。

来自佛罗里达州的马斯特众议员和来自密歇根州的穆勒纳尔众议员在写给财政部长斯科特·贝森特(Scott Bessent)和国务卿马尔科·卢比奥(Marco Rubio)的信中说：“美国人正在遭受网络诈骗，其频率极高且不断攀升，这主要归咎于盘踞在东南亚的中国跨国犯罪组织网络。这些犯罪集团建立了工业级的园区，专门从事复杂的网络诈骗活动，其中包括常被称为‘杀猪盘’的加密货币投资骗局。这些活动利用恋爱诈骗及其他极具破坏性的心理操控手段，榨取美国人的善意与好心。”

他们在信中还指出，缅甸、柬埔寨和老挝的腐败高官对如此惊人规模的犯罪活动视而不见。

两位共和党众议员在信中赞扬了特朗普行政当局打击诈骗犯罪分子及其外国助推者的努力，包括制裁、刑事起诉、扣押资产和悬赏缉捕。他们在信中列出了26名外国个人与两家外国实体--福利来集体公司(Fully Light Group of Companies)和白沙皇宫赌场(White Sands Palace Casino)。两位议员表示，有可信的信息显示，这些个人与实体与东南亚诈骗产业内的网络诈骗中心运作有关联。马斯特和穆勒纳尔要求行政当局展开调查，并在180天内决定这些外国人员是否符合相关法律规定的实施制裁标准。

这封信还抄送给美国司法部长托德·布兰奇(Todd Blanche)与国土安全部长马克韦恩·马林(Markwayne Mullin)。

穆勒纳尔在星期三的一份声明中提到，今年早些时候，他领导的众议院中国问题特设委员会完成了对与中国有关联的庞大诈骗中心网络的[两党调查](https://www.voachinese.com/a/house-select-committee-exposes-china-linked-scam-centers-targeting-americans-20260519/8151690.html) ，并公布了题为《犯罪、腐败与权力：针对美国人并威胁美国安全的与中共有关联的诈骗网络的崛起》的两党报告。

这份报告称，该网络每年至少诈骗美国人100亿美元，同时助长人口贩运、网络犯罪和非法金融活动。报告指出，这些诈骗中心集中在东南亚，特别是柬埔寨和缅甸，是一个分布式犯罪生态系统的一部分，把网络诈骗、人口贩运和洗钱串联在一起。

报告得出结论认为，虽然这些犯罪网络不受国家直接控制，也不是国家支持的阴谋网，但是中国的治理和执法模式为其扩展提供了助力。报告说，这些犯罪网络在很大程度上依托中国的地下银行网络、假币货币中间商和空壳公司，以跨境转移资金并进行洗钱。

众议院外交委员会在星期二的一份声明中提到，去年12月，马斯特领导的众议院外委会通过了《瓦解外国诈骗集团法案》(Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act)。该法案如获最终通过，将以法律化的形式加强跨机构协调并强化美国政府对诈骗中心危机的回应。

按照美国立法程序，一部法案须由众议院和参议院分别经全院通过文字一致的版本，并由总统签署，方能成为法律。

title: How to Navigate Taiwan’s Security Dilemma?
summary: Under Xi Jinping, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has sped up [military modernization](https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/JIPA/Display/Article/3371474/the-ambitious-dragon-beijings-calculus-for-invading-taiwan-by-2030/) while intensifyin
content:
Under Xi Jinping, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has sped up [military modernization](https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/JIPA/Display/Article/3371474/the-ambitious-dragon-beijings-calculus-for-invading-taiwan-by-2030/) while intensifying [military](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-launches-live-firing-drills-around-taiwan-its-biggest-war-games-date-2025-12-30/), [economic](https://jamestown.org/program/power-of-the-weak-taiwans-strategy-in-countering-chinas-economic-coercion/), and [cognitive pressure campaigns](https://globaltaiwan.org/2024/07/countering-cognitive-warfare-taiwans-defense-against-party-influence-in-kinmen/) against Taiwan. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump’s [transactional](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/25/world/asia/taiwan-40-billion-military-trump.html) approach to foreign policy has generated concerns in Taiwan regarding the consistency and predictability of the US commitments. Furthermore, a [divided government](https://thediplomat.com/2026/02/taiwans-protracted-fight-over-the-defense-budget/) has complicated the efforts of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) to formulate and implement long-term security policies—as seen when the Kuomintang (KMT)-led opposition blocked Lai’s [USD 40 billion](https://taiwantoday.tw/Politics/Top-News/278281/President-Lai-announces-NT%241.25-trillion-in-special-defense-spending) special defense budget six times before a reduced [USD 26 billion](https://focustaiwan.tw/politics/202605290009) version passed in May 2026. Taiwan’s security challenge is a question of deterrence, political identity, and policymaking. But measures to strengthen Taiwan’s security will likely intensify domestic polarization or increase the risk of escalation. Therefore, Taiwan needs to increase its resilience and strength without triggering conflict.

In this regard,three mutually reinforcing efforts shape Taiwan’s security resilience: (1) institutionalizing asymmetric deterrence; (2) diversifying security partnerships; and (3) rebuilding domestic political consensus.

**_Institutionalizing Asymmetric Deterrence_**

Given the PRC’s superior military capabilities, Taiwan cannot compete in a conventional manner. Therefore, through the strategy of [asymmetric deterrence](https://doi.org/10.2307/2600829), Taiwan should seek to exploit the vulnerabilities of a superior adversary through dispersed, survivable, and cost-effective capabilities. This concept is not new. In 2008, William Murray first [proposed](https://digital-commons.usnwc.edu/nwc-review/vol61/iss3/3) the “Porcupine Strategy”—whereby Taiwan should make an invasion prohibitively costly rather than match the PRC weapon-for-weapon. This was adopted and formalized in Taiwan’s [2017 National Defense Report](https://www.andrewerickson.com/2017/12/republic-of-china-taiwan-ministry-of-national-defense-issues-2017-national-defense-report/). Additionally,Taiwan’s then-Chief of the General Staff, Admiral Lee Hsi-ming (李喜明), introduced in 2018 the “[Overall Defense Concept](https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/JIPA/Display/Article/4164821/taiwans-defense-policies-in-evolution/)” (ODC)—which divided Taiwan’s forces into two components: a smaller conventional force of major weapons platforms, such as fighter jets, warships and tanks for homeland defense, and a larger asymmetric force of low-cost, mobile and dispersed systems including missile launchers, sea mines and fast-attack craft designed to survive an initial PRC strike and sustain continuous attrition. In doing so, the ODC reframed deterrence as denial, which makes an invasion prohibitively difficult and costly to execute.At the Yushan Forum this year, President Lai [reaffirmed](https://thediplomat.com/2026/03/taiwans-new-southbound-2-0-rewiring-the-indo-pacific-beyond-china/) that Taiwan would accelerate the development of asymmetric capabilities.

Despite the recognized importance of developing asymmetric capabilities, internal [disagreement](https://www.economist.com/special-report/2023/03/06/taiwan-needs-a-new-defence-strategy-to-deal-with-china)s continue among Taiwanese policymakers: chiefly between military traditionalists who favor prestige conventional platforms and reform-minded officials who champion asymmetric systems. This has hindered major steps forward. Moreover, the long reliance on large warships and heavy weaponry has prevented the military’s transformation into a flexible and decentralized asymmetric model, with continuing[considerable resistance](https://indsr.org.tw/uploads/enindsr/files/202512/0a9ed833-9835-4192-9692-7da8dacaffcb.pdf) from internal disagreements.

The events in May demonstrate this challenge:After months of legislative gridlock, the Legislative Yuan (立法院, LY) [passed](https://focustaiwan.tw/politics/202605290009)a special defense budget of USD 26 billion, which occupied around 65 percent of the USD 40 billion that the Lai administration originally [proposed](https://taiwantoday.tw/Politics/Top-News/278281/President-Lai-announces-NT%241.25-trillion-in-special-defense-spending). The approved package concentrated funding on weapons that were approved for sale by the United States; that is, systems cleared through Washington’s [Foreign Military Sales process](https://2017-2021.state.gov/foreign-military-sales-process-and-policy/), under which the State Department and Congress must sign off before American-made arms can be transferred to a foreign government. However, the budget cut allocations for domestic systems, such as indigenous drone production.

The outcome reveals Taiwan’s legislative constraints:lawmakers gravitated toward external platforms over decentralized and made-in-Taiwan asymmetric systems, as had been [envisioned](https://www.airuniversity.af.edu/JIPA/Display/Article/4164821/taiwans-defense-policies-in-evolution/) by Admiral Lee.

To address this issue, the Ministry of National Defense (國防部, MND) should make the case for asymmetric procurement in terms that the LY can evaluate on their own merits, rather than relying on doctrine. For example, the MND can publish comparisons showing how many mobile anti-ship missile batteries or naval mines, priced per unit, could be procured for the cost of a single frigate or fighter jet, alongside estimates of how many PRC vessels or aircraft each option could plausibly deter or destroy. This could shift the debate from abstract doctrine to a metric that every legislator, regardless of party affiliation, can evaluate.

**_Expanding the Network of Security Partners for Deterrence_**

The uncertainty surrounding Trump’s commitments to support Taiwan, and China’s expanding military strength, urges Taiwan to pursue a calibrated strategy of security diversification. This approach could improve intelligence sharing, enhance interoperability in contingency planning, and complicate the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) operational calculations. Furthermore, a broader network of stakeholders interested in cross-Strait stability can increase the political and diplomatic costs of aggression against Taiwan, strengthen deterrence, and reduce the island’s isolation.

The urgency of this diversification was underscored when Acting Secretary of the US Navy Hung Cao [confirmed](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/may/22/us-arms-sales-taiwan-pause-iran-war-says-acting-navy-chief) in May 2026 that Washington had partially suspended pending arms deliveries to Taiwan. Unlike the September 2025 suspension, which critics [attributed](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/09/18/trump-taiwan-arms-sales-military-aid/) to Trump’s trade-off approach toward Beijing, this was cited as a shortage of ammunition following prolonged US military operations against Iran. The lesson for Taiwan remains the same: Washington’s arms deliveries to Taipei depend not only on the island’s political will, but also on the US’s own strategic calculations.

In this regard, cooperation with regional middle powers such as Japan, Australia, and the Philippines should be prioritized, as they share an interest in maintaining stability across the Indo-Pacific.

_(I) Japan_

Japan’s current Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been vocal in forging ties with Taiwan, focusing on [defense commitments](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/editorials/archives/2026/03/05/2003853272). As a large portion of Japan’s energy, resources, and maritime traffic [transit](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/editorials/archives/2025/09/02/2003843060) through the Taiwan Strait, Taiwan’s security is, in essence, closely tied to Japan’s national security. In addition to hardware,[military education exchanges](https://globaltaiwan.org/2022/08/the-future-of-taiwan-japan-defense-cooperation/)—from the cadet to senior-officer level—could diminish Taiwan’s shortfalls in [human capital](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/taiwan/taiwan-doesnt-have-choose), particularly the shortage of volunteer personnel and retention of skilled pilots.This would build shared professional vocabulary and mutual understanding of operational procedures.

Furthermore, both sides need to [strengthen coordination](https://globaltaiwan.org/2022/08/the-future-of-taiwan-japan-defense-cooperation/) in countering China’s grey zone activities through real-time intelligence sharing and analysis, and improve interoperability in missile defense and aerial response,facilitating effective crisis management.

_(II) The Philippines_

Taiwan’s security cooperation with the Philippines has gradually become more salient. Notable activities include [joint patrols](https://tomorrowsaffairs.com/the-discreet-alliance-between-taiwan-and-the-philippines-sets-new-limits-to-chinese-influence) in the Bashi Strait and Taiwan’s [deployment of observers](https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6159862) to the Kamandag military exercise, involving the US and other partners.

Strikingly, the current government of the Philippines has not hidden its desire to collaborate. In July 2025, Philippine Defense Minister Gilbert Teodoro Jr. [said that](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front/archives/2025/07/16/2003840361) “it would be hiding from the obvious to say that Taiwan’s security will not affect us.” Moreover, in May, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. [underlined that](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/05/19/japan/politics/takaichi-marcos-japan-philippines-taiwan/) the Philippines has “no choice” but to be drawn into a Taiwan contingency, expressly stating Manila’s stake in cross-Strait stability.

In late 2025, Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (海洋委員會海巡署) and the Philippine Coast Guard [held a meeting](https://www.navalnews.com/naval-news/2025/12/philippines-and-taiwan-explore-coast-guard-cooperation/) to explore intelligence sharing and capacity building, although lacking a formal and binding framework. Hence, the Lai administration should focus on concrete mechanisms: such as a memorandum of understanding on maritime information sharing, a regular yearly patrol schedule, and an exclusive communication channel during crises.

As America’s close ally, the Philippines has been willing to facilitate US support in a Taiwan contingency. In 2023, under the terms of the _Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement_ (EDCA), Marcos decided to [increase](https://www.csis.org/analysis/transformation-us-philippines-alliance) American military access to strategic bases in the north of the archipelago, particularly in the Cagayan region. Manila also [permitted](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/us-deploys-typhon-missile-launchers-new-location-philippines-2025-01-23/) the US Typhon mid-range missile system to be deployed in Ilocos Norte, which is only 350 km from Taiwan.

_(III) Australia_

Taiwan’s defense cooperation with Australia is more challenging than cooperation with Japan and the Philippines, mainly due to Australia’s caution regarding China’s reaction:Australia’s [_2026 National Defence Strategy_](https://www.defence.gov.au/about/strategic-planning/2026-national-defence-st

title: 末日警告并非人工智能浪潮下的唯一威胁：英美居民还在抗议数据中心
summary: ## 末日警告并非人工智能浪潮下的唯一威胁：英美居民还在抗议数据中心 **末日警告并非人工智能浪潮下的唯一威胁：英美居民还在抗议数据中心** * * ![Image 2](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/ws/160/cpsprodpb/2d88/live/aec02270-b0e6-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png.webp) * Author, 费萨尔·伊斯兰（Faisal Islam） * Role, BBC经济编辑 * P
content:
## 末日警告并非人工智能浪潮下的唯一威胁：英美居民还在抗议数据中心

**末日警告并非人工智能浪潮下的唯一威胁：英美居民还在抗议数据中心**

*       *   ![Image 2](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/ws/160/cpsprodpb/2d88/live/aec02270-b0e6-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png.webp)

    *   Author, 费萨尔·伊斯兰（Faisal Islam）
    *   Role, BBC经济编辑

*   Published 2026年9月16日

*   阅读时间: 6 分钟

数据中心里有一种诡异的低沉嗡鸣声。在那里，数以万计的晶片每秒进行数万亿次运算，推动着人工智能（artificial intelligence, AI；人工智慧）革命的车轮前进。

这些晶片为全球各地向先进人工智能模型发出的查询提供动力，生成文字、图像和视频。

它们的运算，本质上是构成晶片（芯片）的微型硅晶体管不断开合的过程，实际上是无声的。但与所有电脑一样，为这一过程提供动力的大量电力，几乎每一瓦最终都以热能的形式散出，而你听到的声音，正是数千台风扇缓慢运转的嗡鸣——它们的作用是防止热量烧毁成排的服务器机架。

视乎场地规模，你还可能听到变电站中输送电力的变压器发出的嗡嗡声。

](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/ws/640/cpsprodpb/14b9/live/89e5d0e0-b117-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg.webp)

图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，位于英格兰赫特福德郡（Hertfordshire）的这座正在建设中的谷歌（Google）数据中心等设施，正在英国各地变得越来越普遍。

近日来，关于人类面临威胁的惊人警告甚嚣尘上，但真正引发反弹的却是这些低沉的嗡鸣声——这场反弹正在美国发酵，如今已威胁到其国会中期选举，并可能跨越大西洋蔓延至英国。

在美国，对数据中心的反对声音在政治左翼中最为公开。民主党参议员伯尼·桑德斯（Bernie Sanders）呼吁暂停一切新的数据中心建设。

桑德斯告诉我：“人们环顾四周，忧心忡忡——担心这项技术发展得有多快，担心自己对它的掌控力有多小，担心数据中心会如何影响自己所在社区的电价和水资源使用。”

全球人工智能竞赛正以矽谷（Silicon Valley）的最高速度飞速发展，但有可能即将因一些非常本地化的政治和环境问题而受阻。

## 一场有毒辩论

在美国，盖洛普（Gallup）今年5月发布的民调显示，在自己所在区域建数据中心，比建核电站更不受欢迎。就数据中心而言，71%的受访者表示反对，其中48%强烈反对；核电站方面，53%表示反对，其中34%强烈反对。

这种不受欢迎程度在过去两年中不断加深，一些民调显示，半数美国人支持全面暂停数据中心建设。

在英国，部分此类开发项目也遭到了反对——从白金汉郡（Buckinghamshire）、伯克郡（Berkshire）到伦敦东部的红砖巷（Brick Lane），当地居民担心自己所在区域将受到负面影响。

在红砖巷，一个很可能为伦敦金融城（City of London）高频交易商提供服务的数据中心计划，遭到了部分人士的反对，他们更希望看到伦敦东区建设更多社会住房和本地商业项目。

与此同时，在英格兰各郡，对数据中心的巨大需求正带来扩大供给的压力——从斯劳（Slough）一路向绿树成荫的乡村地带延伸。

英国拥有全球第三多的数据中心，中国第二，美国第一。

回到美国，这种反弹也反映在了即将参加11月关键选举的政治人物的言论中。

图像来源，AFP via Getty Images

图像加注文字，能源和水资源方面的压力引发了当地的抗议活动。

这场反弹显然在左翼民主党人中更为明显，但反对数据中心的情绪在共和党支持者中同样清晰可见。一些市议会因其数据中心政策而在选举中被赶下台，而一些州——无论是共和党主导的红州还是民主党主导的蓝州——正在提出禁令。

去年，新泽西州（New Jersey）和弗吉尼亚州（Virginia）的民主党州长之所以能够当选，部分原因正是民众对电价上涨的反弹——而电价上涨被指与数据中心的建设和营运有关。

类似的故事层出不穷：当地小镇居民被要求为新数据中心供电所需的基础设施买单，眼睁睁看着能源账单飙升；或者发现本已紧张的供水进一步减少。由于美国能源系统在地方层面运作，因此帐单上的影响可能立竿见影。

由于美国国会两院的控制权都悬而未决，这种高度地方化的反对力量的规模可能会成为中期选举的决定性因素，进而影响美国政策的走向以及唐纳德·特朗普（Donald Trump；川普）的总统任期。

## 令人眼花撩乱的翻转

今年3月，七大科技巨头的首席执行官与特朗普一同出席签署了“纳税人保护承诺”（Ratepayer Protection Pledge），承诺将“自建、引入或购买”自身所需的能源，并确保成本不会转嫁给“普通家庭”。该承诺不具约束力。

图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，这份承诺几乎没有说服人们接受在自己所在区域建设数据中心。

对一些人来说，这显然还不够。新泽西州和弗吉尼亚州（后者拥有全球规模最大的数据中心集聚区）的新任民主党州长走得更远，通过立法强制为数据中心设立新的能源资费标准，并要求披露能源和水的使用情况。

也许这一切最有力的象征，是德克萨斯州（Texas）亲特朗普的共和党参议院候选人肯·帕克斯顿（Ken Paxton）。他抨击数据中心，在竞选中反对给予其税收减免，并提议：如果相关技术“赋能了损害儿童安全的人工智能聊天机器人”，这些设施的营运商应承担刑事责任。

德克萨斯州曾是最亲商、最亲数据中心、最亲能源产业的州，曾为争夺这类设施展开激烈竞争。例如，它赢得了埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk）旗下 SpaceX 人工智能巨头数十亿美元搬迁投资中的大部分，用于生产人工智能晶片。

图像来源，Getty Images

图像加注文字，肯·帕克斯顿对人工智能采取了强硬立场。

这是一次令人眩晕的转向。人工智能晶片制造商英伟达（Nvidia；辉达）的负责人黄仁勋（Jensen Huang）今年8月登上社交媒体，力陈数据中心是美国再工业化的关键推手。其他科技巨头的首席执行官没有跟进，这或许显示此举在公众眼中颇具争议。

然而，美国的经验表明，谈论对国家经济的整体益处，或潜在的癌症治愈能力，并不总是能引起当地民众的共鸣。数据中心令人感到不安的部分原因在于，这里缺乏真正意义上的常驻员工。

虽然建筑业提供了大量的就业机会，但一个运作正常的数据中心通常只需要数十名员工，即使是规模最大的新建数据中心也只有几百名员工。

要求当地居民接受噪音、彻夜不熄的安保照明，以及对当地能源和水资源供应的压力，并告诉他们这是为了国家利益，这固然容易。但当人工智能公司估值即将突破万亿美元大关，却又预计会造成大规模失业，许多人质疑这项技术是否会将人类从地球上抹去时，要说服他们接受这些措施就难上加难了。

## 关键基础设施

这些争论已经跨越大西洋。在英国斯劳——欧洲最大的数据中心集群——超过500人签署了一份请愿书，称该镇“不应成为一场试验”。他们质疑该镇是否真的从中受益，并要求暂停镇上的数据中心开发。

当地居民抱怨，数据中心产生的热量让本就酷热的夏季气温雪上加霜。有一个项目的选址原本规划用于建设1000套住房，但作为地方议会清偿债务的一部分，被卖给了一家数据中心公司。

回到红砖巷，前工党上议院议员波拉·乌丁女男爵（Baroness Pola Uddin）表示：“我理解建设数据中心的必要性，但必须妥善考虑当地居民的健康与福祉——他们在这里生活、呼吸、上学。我们必须考虑选择更工业化的区域。”

图像来源，AFP via Getty Images

图像加注文字，红砖巷的抗议者们不满他们的社区被利用来服务市政府。

工党政府去年将数据中心列为“关键国家基础设施”（Critical National Infrastructure），这是其加快数据中心部署战略的一部分。

政府认为，数据中心是公共服务的基石，对吸引投资、让英国在全球经济中保持竞争力至关重要。

政府提出的论据是国家经济利益，但政治上的挑战在于当地民众是否愿意忍受。新工党政府上台后的第一批行动之一，就是支持一个位于白金汉郡的数据中心项目——该项目因建在绿化带上而屡遭地方议会拒绝。

大臣们批准了该项目，但随后抗议人士通过众筹发起诉讼，以未考虑环境影响为由提出质疑。政府承认存在错误，撤销了自己的批准，开发商最终承认需要与议会达成具有约束力的清洁能源义务协议。获胜的倡议组织福克斯格洛夫（Foxglove）誓言将把精力重新集中到挑战英国各地其他数据中心项目上。

水是活动人士关注的另一个领域。科技行业辩称，如果考虑到例如管道渗漏损失的水量，他们的用水需求其实并不算大。

在提交给下议院一个委员会的意见书中，行业组织英国水务协会（Water UK）批评政府的人工智能增长战略“对水只字未提”。“似乎存在一种假设，认为这个国家的水资源永远足以满足其经济需求。没有什么比这更离谱的了。”

英国近期扩建数据中心的努力，大多瞄准经过战略性筛选的区域——选址综合考量其对经济的潜在贡献、可供开发的棕地，以及与能源电网和发电设施的现有连接。这些区域被称为“人工智能增长区”（AI Growth zones）。

但即使在这些地方，增长与环境之间的政治平衡也导致内阁内部的拖延。提赛德（Teesside）的一个项目曾引发大臣们之间的拉锯战——争论该地块应用于低碳氢能源项目，还是一座大型新人工智能数据中心。最终，数据中心胜出。

## 环境妥协

矽谷的科技巨头们已经承认，大规模人工智能数据中心的能源需求将导致应对气候变化的进展放缓。英伟达的黄仁勋去年告诉我，当务之急是人工智能本身的发明与部署，他并声称这项技术本身可以帮助解决气候变化问题。“这是在生产智能——还有什么比这更有价值、更重要？”

在英国，仍存在一个根本性问题：一项计划到2030年将现有数据中心容量扩大两倍、达到6吉瓦（gigawatt, GW）持续容量的方案，其电力需求能否与净零排放计划相协调。

预计政府很快将在一份《国家政策声明》（National Policy Statement, NPS）中概述其针对地方政府的数据中心政策，明确哪些类型的项目属于“国家重大项目”，因而有资格由政府加快审批。

自开始起草这份政策声明以来，首相已经换人，围绕这一议题的政治温度也发生了变化。

首相安迪·伯纳姆（Andy Burnham）承诺实现“每个邮编区域都有增长”，而数据中心或许有助于兑现这一承诺。然而，政府在其中扮演的主导角色，也是国家权力集中化的明显例证——这与伯纳姆向地方政府下放更多权力的愿望背道而驰。

这一点，再加上绿党（Green Party）呼吁暂停建设数据中心所带来的挑战，会不会改变安迪·伯纳姆的想法？

## “美国脑袋”

威斯敏斯特的一些人认为，这个议题上存在一种“美国脑袋”（America brain）现象——仅仅因为它在美国是个问题，人们就认为英国也同样如此。

他们表示，当英国正努力达到6吉瓦这一目标时，美国2030年的雄心至少是这个数字的20倍，一些单体超大型项目的规模甚至超过英国的总规划容量。

他们说，对当地电价的影响并不相同——尽管这在一定程度上是因为英国的能源价格本来就更高。

对英国而言，还有一个关乎数据主权的重要论据：避免在支撑服务经济大面积领域的信息技术基础设施上，完全依赖美国或其他国家。

有人谈到，需要汲取本世纪初社交媒体和互联网发展的教训——英国当时未能捕捉到随之而来的经济和政治权力红利，主要是这些技术的使用者，而非制造者。

一位大臣告诉我：“这一次（在人工智能上），我们必须做对，但前提是拥有一定水平的数据基础设施。”英国的雄心被视为相对适度——目标是到2030年，在国民保健服务体系（NHS）、国家安全和金融服务领域实现持续的人工智能应用。

这种“切身利害”的论调在人工智能实验室中得到了呼应。一些有影响力的声音认为，他们的模型对社会的影响将如此深远，以至于会从根本上影响政府征税的能力，尤其是对劳动征税。他们的未来学家畅想着经济中现金流被彻底打乱的图景。实体数据中心或许会成为向这场革命的收益征税的少数途径之一。

在美国，一些曾竭力欢迎数据中心的政客，如今表示自己已经倒戈。税收优惠正在变成税务要求。美国小镇的这种反弹或许具有其独特的美国背景，但也在全球范围内引起了共鸣。

title: Can Human Rights Survive the Era of Great-Power Competition?

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BdE2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F745797da-79cf-4dc5-8728-378a1219fae1_5760x3840.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BdE2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F745797da-79cf-4dc5-8728-378a1219fae1_5760x3840.jpeg)

Pro-democracy protesters in the Mong Kok district of Hong Kong, Oct. 19, 2014. Photo credit: r-monochrome

_THE JAPAN TIMES
July 20, 2026_

**By Michael Judge**

_When I [first interviewed](https://michaeljudge.substack.com/p/what-happens-to-freedom-deferred) Maya Wang in 2024, China’s crackdown on Hong Kong had entered its fourth year, reshaping the global debate on authoritarianism. Since then, wars, geopolitical rivalry and economic competition have increasingly eclipsed human rights as the world’s defining concern._

_As Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director, Wang has become one of the leading figures documenting abuses in China, especially in Hong Kong, Xinjiang and Tibet. Her investigations into mass surveillance, digital authoritarianism and the persecution of ethnic and religious minorities have helped shape international understanding of human rights in the 21st century._

_When we met again at Human Rights Watch’s Tokyo office earlier this month, I asked how human rights have fared in an era increasingly defined by great-power competition — and if she still believes there are reasons for hope._

_— MJ_

**MJ: The last time we spoke, Hong Kong dominated international headlines. Looking back now, what does Hong Kong tell us about where China and the international human rights movement are today?**

**MW:**Actually, I think Hong Kong is a good place to start, because if you think about where we are now with human rights in Hong Kong and its repressive [national security law](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/03/24/asia-pacific/politics/hong-kong-police-phone-computer-passwords/), Hong Kong benefited from that period not long ago when people believed societies like China could liberalize through trade. I think that entire dream is now over.

Hong Kong is on a geopolitical fault line. The national security law, enacted in 2020 and expanded through Hong Kong’s [Article 23 legislation](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2024/03/19/asia-pacific/politics/hong-kong-article-23/) in 2024, also marked the beginning of China’s use of national security laws to shape its interactions with — and influence beyond — its borders. In many ways, Hong Kong is not just a small place. What happens to it tells us something about the future.

I don’t think human rights have simply become marginalized. The international human rights system was a product of World War II. The institutions that came out of that period, including the World Trade Organization, are now all being rethought. There’s pushback against globalization and neoliberalism, both at the popular level and at the government level. The imposition of tariffs marks the end of the “free trade is always good” era.

When China joined the WTO, labor rights were essentially stripped out of trade. Human rights were moved into institutions with very little enforcement power. But legislation like the [Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2021/12/09/world/politics-diplomacy-world/us-house-uyghur-bill/) in the United States adds human rights back into trade.

If democracies adopt legislation like that, they are essentially creating standards for participation in international commerce. Human rights become part of economic policy again.

So while governments today often treat human rights as a lower priority, the reshaping of the international order presents an opportunity. Democracies could seize it — or miss it.

**I used to work for The Wall Street Journal, a paper that has long promoted “free markets and free people.” In places like China, the idea was that if you liberalized markets, politics would follow. People even talked about Hong Kong becoming a Trojan horse. Instead, China became the Trojan horse.**

Exactly. Hong Kong was the Trojan horse that allowed China to enter global trade. China’s political economy is built upon what some scholars call a “low-rights economy.” Communities can be displaced without adequate compensation. Workers cannot organize independent unions. Migrant workers remain second-class citizens.

How do democracies compete with a system that doesn’t bear those social costs? If democracies build those costs back into trade, then they’re leveling the playing field. Human rights are not separate from economics.

**How do artificial intelligence and AI-enabled surveillance fit into that? Does AI simply make authoritarian governments more powerful?**

The issue isn’t only surveillance. Chinese technology develops within a regulatory environment that privileges the collection of data without safeguards. It privileges monitoring and control. It’s not only about whether the government orders companies to do something. It’s about the system those companies emerge from.

Many countries now use both Chinese and Western technology. The key question is whether they have strong privacy laws, transparency requirements and accountability. American companies also collect enormous amounts of data. The difference is that they operate in societies where they can still be investigated, criticized and regulated.

In Europe, for example, Chinese technology still has to comply with the European Union’s strict [General Data Protection Regulation](https://gdpr-info.eu/) law, which sets rigorous standards for how companies collect, store and use personal data. Strong privacy rules make it much harder for those technologies to replicate the surveillance model used inside China. So while Chinese technology is spreading rapidly, regulatory frameworks still matter.

**It doesn’t bode well when the president of the United States is constantly attacking regulations and the foundations of international law. Doesn’t that encourage authoritarian governments to do the same?**

American technology companies already operate in an environment with very limited federal privacy regulation. The United States developed what many scholars call surveillance capitalism.

China has state-led surveillance. The United States has surveillance capitalism. Both raise profound questions about privacy. But they are not equivalent. In China, technology companies are actively recruited into a system of state surveillance. In the United States, you can still expose companies, criticize them publicly and hold them accountable. That distinction matters.

**Myanmar seems to have disappeared from international attention. Are the human rights violations of countries like Myanmar and North Korea falling off the map?**

I think the larger issue is that U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are all sending the same message: Hard power is what matters. Build your economy. Build your military. Protect yourself. That’s the real game. I think that’s a form of international gaslighting.

For countries like Japan, Canada or Australia, international norms matter enormously. Yes, Myanmar and North Korea receive less attention. But that’s because the world has collectively shifted toward realpolitik.

Human rights emerged after World War II because the world witnessed the horrors of Nazi Germany. The question now is whether we have to experience something comparable again before people recognize why those institutions exist.

Young people in Thailand, Myanmar and Hong Kong understand human rights because they’ve had to fight for them. Sadly, people who grow up inside long-established democracies often take them for granted.

**Japan is reevaluating its security in the region because confidence in the Japan-U.S. alliance has weakened. But what role should it play in promoting human rights and defending democratic ideals?**

China views ideology as a security issue. Xi has made that perfectly clear. Document No. 9, a confidential 2013 Chinese Communist Party directive warning against the influence of Western democratic ideas, identifies democracy, universal values and the rule of law as ideological threats.

Ironically, democracies often don’t think of democracy as something requiring active defense. Japan should invest not only in military and economic security but also in protecting democratic values.

My colleagues and I at Human Rights Watch have proposed an Asia Democracy Fund. Human rights defenders across Asia have become increasingly vulnerable. Democracies could pool resources to support them. . . .

**People often forget that the 1989 Tiananmen movement wasn’t only students; workers also played an enormous role. As AI and automation replace workers, do ordinary people risk losing political power?**

The traditional idea of workers has changed. People no longer work together in one factory their entire lives. Gig workers are isolated. Hannah Arendt wrote that totalitarianism thrives on atomized people, and automation can deepen that isolation.

But new forms of solidarity are emerging. One of the brightest examples in China is feminism. Many highly educated young women increasingly recognize the structural inequalities they face, and because of that they often sympathize with many other human rights causes. They’ve played leading roles in movements ranging from the [White Paper](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2022/11/28/asia-pacific/china-blank-sheet-protest-symbol/) protests [the 2022 demonstrations against COVID-19 restrictions] to animal-rights campaigns.

Every movement creates new activists. There’s reason for hope, even in what might feel like hopeless times.

_Michael Judge is Opinion editor of The Japan Times. This interview was edited for length and clarity._

title: Opinion | Why more export controls won’t stop China’s industrial engine
summary: The first “China shock” was fairly easy to understand. Beginning in the 1990s, cheap Chinese goods poured into global markets, displacing large parts of lower-end manufacturing across the world. Now, [China shock 2.0](https://www.scmp.com/n
content:
The first “China shock” was fairly easy to understand. Beginning in the 1990s, cheap Chinese goods poured into global markets, displacing large parts of lower-end manufacturing across the world. Now, [China shock 2.0](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3355120/european-leaders-get-ready-act-now-amid-rising-fears-china-shock-20?module=inline&pgtype=article) seems to be under way, with China taking the lead in electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, solar panels, semiconductors and other more technologically sophisticated industries.

This is often perceived as a trade problem, with Chinese manufacturers producing too much, selling too cheaply and [flooding global markets](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/economics/article/3277522/southeast-asias-struggle-stay-afloat-amid-flood-cheap-chinese-imports?module=inline&pgtype=article) with subsidised goods. However, the more consequential question is not just why the United States and Europe run growing trade deficits with China. It is who is supplying the next round of industrial growth in Asia, Africa, Latin America and other emerging markets. That makes today’s industrial competition more of a production story than a trade story.

Headlines on the technological race between China and the US are usually about the frontier: [artificial intelligence](https://www.scmp.com/topics/artificial-intelligence?module=inline&pgtype=article) (AI), advanced semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology and other fields in which scientific leadership could determine the future. China’s efforts to catch up with the technological and productivity frontier can make it look like the country’s industrial future lies entirely at the highest end of technology.

However, much of China’s industrial expansion is happening in a different area: technologies that are less cutting edge but already proven and widely used throughout the world.

Much of the modern economy does not run on frontier technology. Rather, it relies on mature technologies that are reliable, affordable and fit for the job. China is becoming one of the main suppliers of that kind of proven technology.

Automobiles show why industrial competition is not just about the frontier. German industrial strength has never depended on producing every German car inside Germany. By 2010, German carmakers were already producing more vehicles abroad than at home. Much of the production shift has been visible in China and the so-called German-Central European supply chain.

Volkswagen employees work on the assembly line for its ID.3 electric car at the company’s “Transparent Factory” production site in Dresden, eastern Germany, on May 14, 2025. Photo: AFP

China presents a different challenge. It is not that German manufacturers are incapable of producing electric cars; Germany still remains a major EV producer. Rather, electrification has changed the source of much of the value, technology and strategic dependence. While the internal combustion vehicle rewarded decades of German expertise in engines, transmissions and mechanical engineering, EVs rely more heavily on batteries, semiconductors, software and digital architecture. Germany might still produce EVs, but a growing share of the components on which those cars depend now comes from China.

The EV race is not just about having the latest technology. China’s battery dominance has been built in large part around [lithium iron phosphate](https://www.scmp.com/business/companies/article/3154120/how-do-electric-vehicle-batteries-work-and-why-do-they-sometimes?module=inline&pgtype=article) technology, a mature technology that is cost effective, reliable and suitable for mass-market vehicles.

Automobiles also depend on mature chips. A Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago report estimates that an average internal combustion vehicle contains more than 1,000 semiconductors, around 95 per cent of which are mature or legacy chips. EVs use more sophisticated processors, but they still rely heavily on mature chips alongside other proven technologies such as batteries, software and digital architecture. These are precisely the areas in which China has built a dense domestic ecosystem.

09:10

Can the Middle East war turbocharge China’s global EV ambitions?

The semiconductor industry consists of much more than frontier processors. China’s share of global capacity for mature chips has expanded dramatically: it has grown three to four times during the past decade, rising from about 17 per cent in 2015 to 33 per cent in 2024 and a projected 45 per cent in 2027. Such chips will not power the most advanced AI models or [graphics cards](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-war/article/3310317/nvidias-consumer-graphics-cards-see-price-hikes-china-after-h20-sales-ban?module=inline&pgtype=article), but they do perform many of the less spectacular but key functions without which the modern economy cannot operate.

China [subsidising its industries](https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-economy/article/3167588/chinas-industrial-subsidies-what-are-they-and-why-are-they?module=inline&pgtype=article) is far from a new development, and the use of subsidies, tax incentives and below-market borrowing are hardly unique to China. What makes China different is partly where the money has gone.

Financing technology-intensive industries does not necessarily mean financing only the most cutting-edge technologies. In fact, much of China’s capital is going into technologies that are already mature. Since 2021, China’s semiconductor industry has made more than US$75 billion in new investment, primarily in legacy technology nodes. China is competing in the race for advanced chips, but it is also pouring capital into the less glamorous technologies on which much of the industrial economy already depends.

The central story is that the modern industrial economy does not simply replace mature technologies with frontier ones. Mature technologies are not obsolete technologies. They are becoming increasingly important to China’s position in the global industry as machinery, electrical equipment and transport equipment now account for more than half of the country’s exports. China is also exporting more of these products to emerging markets, [especially within Southeast Asia](https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3360517/chinas-power-exports-asean-surge-40-first-half-2026-amid-hormuz-tensions?module=inline&pgtype=article).

Now, the US and European responses to China still focus on controlling what enters their markets, but the deeper challenge is production capacity. Tariffs might keep some Chinese goods out of American or European markets, and export controls might slow China’s progress in some frontier technologies. However, neither does much to prevent Chinese machinery, components and capital goods from replacing Western products in emerging markets.

The key question is not simply who invents the technologies of tomorrow; it is who produces, adapts and scales the mature technologies that the modern economy already runs on today. A country can remain at the scientific frontier while losing the ability to manufacture the technologies that support it.

China’s manufacturing model makes one thing clear: industrial competition requires both innovation at the frontier and the ecosystems needed to produce proven technologies that support the industrial economy.

title: Japan's Takaichi set to signal policy continuity in cabinet reshuffle
summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi holds a press conference at the Prime Minister’s Office, as cabinet support falls, following the close of the 221st extraordinary session of the Diet, in Tokyo, Japan, July 27, 2026. David Mareuil/Pool
content:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi holds a press conference at the Prime Minister’s Office, as cabinet support falls, following the close of the 221st extraordinary session of the Diet, in Tokyo, Japan, July 27, 2026. David Mareuil/Pool via REUTERS/ File Photo [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/pm-takaichi-holds-press-conference-as-cabinet-support-falls/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMjlNTUFTT0pYTA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

*   Summary

*   Takaichi seen reappointing Finance Minister Katayama
*   PM's reflationist ally Kiuchi seen keeping post, Yomiuri says
*   Lack of big change signals policy continuity
*   New line-up suggests little change to Takaichi's spending plans

TOKYO, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is set to retain key ministers in a cabinet ​reshuffle on Thursday, while looking to shore up political support to push through her flagship spending plans amid jittery ‌financial markets.

In her first reshuffle since taking office last October, Takaichi is likely to retain Satsuki Katayama as finance minister, [sources have told Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-pm-keep-finance-minister-cabinet-reshuffle-mainichi-reports-2026-09-03/), a move that will ensure continuity in Japan's exchange-rate policy.

Make sense of global markets with the Trading Day newsletter. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/trading-day/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fworld%2Fasia-pacific%2Fjapans-takaichi-set-signal-policy-continuity-cabinet-reshuffle-2026-09-16%2F)

Katayama played a key role negotiating with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on a rare joint US-Japan yen intervention in late July, ​an effort that underscored the countries' close cooperation.

The reappointment of Katayama, a former finance ministry bureaucrat seen as taking a conservative ​view on fiscal policy, is likely to be welcomed by bond markets wary of Takaichi's expansionary fiscal approach ⁠that could boost debt issuance, analysts say.

"Rather than going for stronger appeal on her policy colour, Takaichi is likely prioritising policy continuity and ​stability to lay the groundwork for re-appointment in the ruling party leadership race in September next year," said Takahide Kiuchi, an economist at Nomura ​Research Institute.

Concern over prospects for Japan's worsening finances has sent the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) to three-decade highs this week, as public debt, at twice the size of its economy, is the largest among advanced nations.

## NO INTENTION OF REINING IN BIG SPENDING PLANS

In a sign that she has no intention ​of reining in her big spending plans, however, Takaichi is also likely to keep her reflationist ally Minoru Kiuchi as economic revitalisation minister, the [Yomiuri](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-pm-retain-kiuchi-economy-minister-cabinet-reshuffle-yomiuri-reports-2026-09-15/) newspaper ​said on Thursday.

Such choices highlight the tricky balancing act Takaichi faces. With households smarting from a rising cost of living, she risks hurting her approval ratings ‌by backing ⁠down on her pledge to cut tax and boost spending.

But she is also under pressure to heed market calls for fiscal discipline, after her ambitious spending plans and a decision to pursue a two-year [tax cut](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-sidestep-funding-tax-cut-outline-keep-fiscal-concern-alive-2026-09-15/) on food items sparked a bond sell-off and [criticism](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-faces-day-policy-reckoning-bessent-calls-time-big-stimulus-2026-09-01/) from Bessent.

Domestic media have said Takaichi is set to retain other key ministers, including some of her competitors in last year's race to lead the ruling party, such ​as Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and ​Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.

As head ⁠of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), she also roughly maintained the line-up of party executives on Wednesday in a sign of her focus on political continuity.

Takaichi is expected to give a cabinet post to the ​LDP's coalition partner Japan Innovation Party, looking to solidify the two parties' policy cooperation.

## OPPOSITION SET TO GRILL ​GOVT ON FUNDING

The ⁠new cabinet will head into parliament debate over key fiscal issues such as legislation for a two-year cut in [sales tax](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-sidestep-funding-tax-cut-outline-keep-fiscal-concern-alive-2026-09-15/) on food items, with opposition parties expected to grill the administration over how to fund it.

Takaichi's [pledge](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-aims-cap-fy27-new-bond-issuance-40-trillion-yen-pm-says-yomiuri-interview-2026-08-28/) to cap new government bond issuance around 40 trillion yen ($256.1 billion) for the fiscal ⁠2027 budget ​is already facing scrutiny, with expenditure seen increasing from [budget requests](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/japan-budget-requests-swell-pandemic-era-scale-under-takaichi-agenda-2026-09-04/) that swelled to pandemic-era ​scale.

Japan also faces the prospects of higher defence spending in a strategy review this year.

The cost of funding Japan's debt is increasing as the central bank raises interest rates ​and slows bond purchases in an effort to wean the economy off decades of massive stimulus.

($1=156.1700 yen)

Reporting by Leika Kihara; Editing by Clarence Fernandez
